p: Apokalypsis means pulling the cover off. One unveiling, singular, and it is of Jesus.
b: The oldest manuscripts call the book "the Apocalypse of John." Apokalypsis means an unveiling, like pulling a cover off something. It is one unveiling, singular, so the title is "Revelation," not "Revelations." The book's own first words call it "the unveiling of Jesus Christ" (1:1). It is first about who Jesus is, and only then about events.

p: "Soon" or "quickly"? Every view has to explain this word.
b: En tachei and tachy can mean "soon" or "quickly." Preterists read "soon for the first readers." Many futurists read "swiftly, once it starts," or "soon on God's clock" (2 Peter 3:8). "The time is near" (1:3; 22:10) is harder to stretch, and every view has to explain it. The phrase "what must happen" comes from Daniel 2:28–29, 45 in the Greek, where it is what will happen "in the last days." John writes "soon" instead, and Beale and Bauckham see the point: what Daniel saw far off has already begun. The same phrase returns in 1:19 and 4:1.
orig: ἐν τάχει (en tachei); ταχύ (tachy); ὁ καιρὸς ἐγγύς (ho kairos engys)

p: Doulos is the word for a slave. In the Bible, "slave of God" was also a title of honor.
b: A doulos was a slave: a person owned by someone else, as a large share of the people in the cities of Roman Asia were. Slaves could be household managers, teachers or field hands, and some members of the seven churches were surely slaves themselves. The Greek Old Testament calls Moses, David and the prophets God's douloi (Joshua 14:7; 2 Samuel 7:5; Amos 3:7), so "slave of God" was an honor, not a shame: it meant belonging wholly to the true master. Many English Bibles say "servant," following the King James tradition and avoiding the picture of slavery in American history, which differed from Roman slavery in important ways. This site keeps "slave," as in Jude 1:1, so the reader feels the claim of ownership. John calls himself one (1:1), and so are all the faithful (2:20; 7:3; 22:3).

p: "Made known," with a hint of "signs": Beale hears "sign-ified," shown in pictures.
b: Sēmainō usually just means "make known, indicate" (John 12:33; Acts 11:28), so the Plain says "made it known." The KJV's "signified" keeps the root, sēma, "sign," and some scholars (Beale) hear "sign-ified": made known by symbols, as in Daniel 2:45 in the Greek, where God made the future known through a statue in a dream. Whether or not the word carries that hint, the book soon shows that it speaks in pictures.

a: reads the words of this prophecy out loud
t: A book meant to be heard
p: One person read it aloud to the whole church. Most listeners could not read.
b: Ancient letters were read aloud in the assembly (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27). The blessing is for "the one who reads" (singular) and "those who hear" (plural). Revelation's repeated patterns of sevens, threes and echoes help a listening audience follow it. It is the first of seven "blessed" sayings in the book.

a: who is, who was, and who is coming
p: A Greek expansion of "I AM WHO I AM" from Exodus 3:14.
b: John breaks Greek grammar here: after "from" he writes the name in the nominative case, as if the name cannot be changed. The phrase unfolds Exodus 3:14 ("I AM"), which Jewish interpreters already read as "the one who was, is, and will be." Notice that John says "is coming," not "will be." God's future is an arrival.

p: Probably the Holy Spirit in full, with seven as completeness.
b: The greeting comes from the Father, the seven Spirits, and Jesus Christ, which looks like an early picture of the Trinity. The seven Spirits are later called seven torches (4:5) and the Lamb's seven eyes (5:6), from Zechariah 4:2, 10. Some read them as seven chief angels instead (compare 8:2). Isaiah 11:2 lists the Spirit's gifts (seven in the Greek Old Testament).

a: the ruler of the kings of the earth
p: Three titles of Jesus from one psalm about David’s king.
b: "Firstborn" and "most high over the kings of the earth" come from Psalm 89:27, and "faithful witness" echoes Psalm 89:37, "the witness in the skies is faithful." In a world where Caesar claimed to rule the kings of the earth, the opening greeting names a different ruler.

t: Israel’s calling, now given to the church
p: "A kingdom of priests" was God’s word to Israel at Mount Sinai.
b: Exodus 19:6 calls Israel "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation." Revelation applies the phrase to everyone Jesus freed by his blood, "from every tribe and language" (5:9). Some see the church taking up Israel's role; others see Gentiles joining Israel's calling, not replacing it (Romans 11:17). Peter does the same with this verse (1 Peter 2:9).

a: He is coming with the clouds
p: A worldwide return, or Christ’s judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70?
b: The verse joins Daniel 7:13 (the son of man coming on clouds) with Zechariah 12:10 (they will look on the one they pierced). Futurists read the visible return of Christ to the whole world. Preterists note that in the Old Testament God rides on a cloud to judge a nation (Isaiah 19:1) and read the judgment of Jerusalem. Jesus joins the same two passages in his talk on the Mount of Olives: "all the tribes of the earth will mourn" when they see the Son of Man coming on the clouds (Matthew 24:30). At his trial he joined Daniel 7:13 with Psalm 110:1 instead (Matthew 26:64).

p: The Greek Old Testament of Zechariah 12:10 has a different verb. John, like the Gospel of John, says "pierced."
b: In Zechariah 12:10 the Hebrew says they will look on the one they "pierced" (daqaru). The Septuagint read the letters differently and says they "danced in triumph" or "mocked." Revelation uses exekentēsan, "pierced," the same word as John 19:37, "They will look at the one they pierced," where the soldier's spear fulfills the verse. So John here translates from the Hebrew, or uses a Greek version closer to it, not the usual Septuagint.

a: All the tribes of the earth
t: "All kindreds of the earth," or of the land?
p: Gē means both "earth" and "land." Which one changes the whole verse.
b: Gē means both "earth" and "land." The verse quotes Zechariah 12:10–12, where the mourners are the families of Israel. Preterists read "all the tribes of the land" and see first-century Judea. Futurists read "all the peoples of the earth" and see a worldwide return. Both are possible Greek.
orig: πᾶσαι αἱ φυλαὶ τῆς γῆς (pasai hai phylai tēs gēs)

p: "The Almighty" is the Greek Old Testament’s word for "the LORD of Armies" and for Shaddai.
b: Pantokratōr means "ruler of all." The Septuagint uses it for the Hebrew title this site renders "the LORD of Armies" (YHWH tseva'ot), and sometimes for Shaddai, "the Almighty." Outside 2 Corinthians 6:18, it appears in the New Testament only in Revelation (nine times). This site says "the Almighty" in all nine places, as most English Bibles do and as it does for Shaddai and in Judith, so the title is easy to follow across the Bible. It means more than strong: the one who holds all things in his hand. Roman emperors were sometimes praised as rulers of the world. Revelation reserves the word for God.

p: A rocky island off Asia Minor, used by Rome for exile.
b: Patmos is about 13 square miles. Banishment to an island was a known Roman punishment. Irenaeus (about AD 180) dates the vision to the end of Domitian's reign (Against Heresies 5.30.3). Clement of Alexandria says John came back from the island after "the tyrant" died, without naming him, and Eusebius (Church History 3.18) and Victorinus say plainly that Domitian banished him. "The suffering... and the endurance" he shares with the readers are what the whole book asks of them.

t: "The testimony of Jesus": his, or about him?
p: The testimony Jesus gave, or the testimony believers give about him? The Greek allows both.
b: The phrase comes five times (1:2, 9; 12:17; 19:10; 20:4). Read one way, it is the witness Jesus himself bore, "the faithful witness" (1:5), which John passes on (1:2). Read the other way, it is the believers' witness about Jesus, the reason John is on Patmos and the martyrs die (6:9; 20:4). Many scholars think John means both: the testimony Jesus gave, which his followers keep holding to and repeating (Bauckham; compare 19:10, "the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy"). The Plain keeps "the testimony of Jesus" every time, so the reader can weigh it. The word family martys, "witness," runs through the whole book: Jesus, Antipas (2:13), the two witnesses (11:3), and the martyrs.

t: "The Lord’s day" is not "the Day of the Lord"
p: Sunday, the day of the resurrection, not "the Day of the Lord."
b: Kyriakē is an adjective: "the Lord's." Early Christian writers used it for Sunday, the day of the resurrection (Didache 14; Ignatius, To the Magnesians 9). A few readers take it as "the Day of the Lord," the end times. Greek writes that phrase differently: hēmera kyriou (1 Thessalonians 5:2).
orig: ἐν τῇ κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ (en tē kyriakē hēmera)

a: one like a son of man
p: From Daniel 7:13, Jesus’s favorite name for himself.
b: In Daniel 7 "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom. John then describes him with features Daniel gives to God himself (white hair, 7:9) and to the angel of Daniel 10:5–6 (gold belt, fiery eyes, bronze legs). The robe and sash are the clothes of a priest (Exodus 28:4).

t: The Ancient of Days walks among the lamps
p: Jesus is given God’s own portrait, then put to work as the temple priest.
b: Daniel 7:9 gives white wool hair to the Ancient of Days, God. John's figure also wears a priest's robe and walks among lampstands, the priest's daily job of trimming the temple lamps (Exodus 27:20–21; Leviticus 24:1–4). My reading: the vision says both "he is God" and "he tends the churches like a priest tends lamps," trimming, refilling, and, if needed, removing one (2:5). The priestly-lamp reading is held by several scholars (e.g. Beale); the link to the threat in 2:5 is my emphasis.

t: "Polished bronze": a word found nowhere else
p: No other Greek text uses this word, so no one is sure what metal John means.
b: Chalkolibanon appears only here and in 2:18. It seems to join chalkos, "copper, bronze," with a second part that may be libanos, "frankincense" (perhaps for its color), or a word for a furnace or for refined metal. Guesses include fine bronze, brass, an alloy of gold and silver, or a local metal: Thyatira, where 2:18 repeats the word, had a guild of bronze workers. "Polished bronze" gives the likely sense, a bright metal glowing as if just out of the furnace, as in Daniel 10:6 and Ezekiel 1:7.

a: a sharp two-edged sword was coming out of his mouth
p: His weapon is his word.
b: Isaiah 49:2: "He made my mouth a sharp sword." Isaiah 11:4: "the breath of his lips will put the wicked to death." Hebrews 4:12 says God's word cuts more sharply than any two-edged sword. Revelation's last battle is won by this sword alone (19:15, 21).

p: In Isaiah, "the first and the last" means "there is no other God."
b: Isaiah 44:6: "I am first, and I am last," and there is no god but him. The Lord God calls himself "the Alpha and the Omega" in 1:8, and Jesus says "I am the First and the Last" here and in 22:13. Revelation gives Jesus the titles of God alone.

a: the keys of Death and of Hades
p: Greek religion gave these keys to Hecate or Aeacus. Jewish teachers gave them to God alone.
b: In Greek and Roman belief the keeper of the underworld's keys was a god such as Hecate or Aeacus, and Hades was the god of the dead. A closer parallel is Jewish: the rabbis taught that God kept three keys in his own hand and gave them to no agent, the keys of rain, of childbirth and of raising the dead (Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 2a), and the Targum Neofiti on Genesis 30:22 lists the key of the graves among God's keys. Verdict: John's first readers in Ephesus, where Hecate was worshiped, may have heard a challenge to her, but the claim itself comes from the Jewish picture: Jesus, who was dead, holds keys that belong to God alone. Compare Matthew 16:18–19.

a: what you saw, what is, and what is going to happen after this
p: Many futurists see three parts here: past, present, future.
b: Futurists often read: "what you saw" = chapter 1; "what is" = chapters 2–3; "what is going to happen after this" = 4–22, still future. Others read two parts, "what you saw, that is, what is and what is going to happen" (Beale), or a phrase meaning "everything," since the visions mix past, present and future throughout. A third option takes "what is" as "what they mean," the sense the same Greek verb has in the next verse ("the seven stars are angels," 1:20; Aune, Beale). "What is going to happen after this" echoes Daniel 2:28–29, 45 in the Greek; see the note on "soon" at 1:1.

p: Angelos means "messenger": an angel, or a human leader?
b: Angelos simply means "messenger." The "angels of the seven churches" may be guardian angels, or human leaders who read the letters aloud. Each letter scolds its "angel" for the church's sins, which some think fits a human pastor better.

p: The greatest city of Asia, home of the temple of Artemis.
b: A port of perhaps 200,000 people. Paul worked there over two years (Acts 19) and warned its elders about false teachers (Acts 20:29–30). The letter praises them for testing false apostles. Tradition says John lived there late in life.

a: you have let your first love go
p: Love for Jesus, love for each other, or both?
b: The Greek just says "your first love." Readers debate whether it means love for Christ, love for fellow believers (which can grow cold in a church busy fighting error), or the early zeal of their conversion. The cure is to "do again the works you did at the start" (2:5), which suggests actions, not only feelings.

p: Ephesus’s harbor silted up. The city’s site has moved over the centuries.
b: The river Cayster kept filling Ephesus's harbor with silt, and the city had to move more than once. Today the ruins stand miles from the sea. Ancient readers would also have known the temple lamps that a priest could take away. Most read the threat as the end of a church's life and witness, not as a statement about individual salvation; how far a believer can fall away is a question the traditions answer differently (see the topic on perseverance).

p: Probably Christians who said joining in idol feasts was fine.
b: Irenaeus (about AD 180) linked them to Nicolaus, one of the seven deacons (Acts 6:5), though that may be guesswork. The letters connect them with "the teaching of Balaam" (2:14–15). Nikolaos means "conquers the people," and Balaam was explained in Hebrew as "swallows the people," so the two names may be a pair.

p: The first promise of the book points to the last chapter.
b: Genesis 3:22–24 closes the way to the tree of life. Revelation 22:2 shows it again, beside the river. The promises to the seven churches are all fulfilled in chapters 19–22. At Ephesus, where Artemis's temple stood in a sacred grove, the "paradise of God" is a pointed contrast.

p: A short, limited trial, as in Daniel 1.
b: Daniel and his friends were tested for ten days (Daniel 1:12–15). Ten days is a short, measured time with an end. Historicists have read it as ten years of Diocletian's persecution (303–313), or ten Roman persecutions.

p: Smyrna’s ring of hilltop buildings was called its "crown."
b: Ancient writers described the buildings around Mount Pagos as Smyrna's crown. The word here is stephanos, a victor's wreath, not a king's diadem. Smyrna's bishop Polycarp was later burned there (about AD 155).

p: KJV "seat" is thronos, the word used for God’s throne.
b: KJV says "seat." The word is thronos, the same word Revelation uses over 40 times for God's throne. Pergamum had a giant altar of Zeus and was the first city in Asia with a temple to Rome and Augustus (29 BC). The picture is political: two thrones, and you must pick one.
orig: ὁ θρόνος τοῦ Σατανᾶ (ho thronos tou Satana)

p: The prophet who could not curse Israel, so he taught them to sin.
b: In Numbers 22–24 Balaam is hired to curse Israel but can only bless them. Numbers 31:16 says his advice later led Israel to sin with Moabite women and idols at Peor (Numbers 25). Balaam became a byword for selling out God's people for gain (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11).

p: A jar of manna was kept in the ark, which went missing.
b: Exodus 16:33–34: a jar of manna was kept before the LORD. Jewish tradition said Jeremiah hid the ark (2 Maccabees 2:4–8) and that the Messiah would bring the manna back (2 Baruch 29:8). Those who refuse idol feasts will get heaven's food instead. Compare John 6:31–35.

p: Jurors voted "not guilty" with white stones. Stones were also feast tickets.
b: Several customs fit: a white pebble for acquittal in court; inscribed tokens that admitted guests to banquets; amulets carrying a secret name. All suit Pergamum, a city of courts and feasts. Some also connect the high priest's stones engraved with names (Exodus 28:9–12).

p: A nickname from the queen who led Israel into Baal worship.
b: Queen Jezebel promoted the worship of Baal (1 Kings 16:31; 21:25) and opposed Elijah. The woman at Thyatira probably was a real prophet in the church whom John calls by this name, the way we might call someone "a Judas." Her teaching seems to have allowed members to join guild feasts honoring the gods.

p: The Bible’s phrase for a person’s hidden feelings and thoughts, from Jeremiah 17:10.
b: In Hebrew thought the kidneys were the seat of the deepest feelings and the heart the seat of thought and will. In Jeremiah 17:10 the LORD says he searches the heart and tests the kidneys, to give each person what their ways deserve. Jesus takes that claim for himself, with the same promise to repay "according to your works." English Bibles usually say "minds and hearts" or "hearts and minds"; the Greek keeps the body picture.

t: "The deep things": a slogan turned around
p: They likely said "the deep things of God." Jesus corrects the label.
b: Paul writes that the Spirit searches "the deep things of God" (1 Corinthians 2:10). Many scholars suggest the Thyatira group claimed secret, deeper knowledge, perhaps arguing that a mature Christian could enter an idol's temple unharmed. That they said "the deep things of God" and Jesus swaps in "of Satan" is a standard proposal (Charles, Mounce, Aune and others discuss it). My addition is only the pattern: the swap works the way the letters elsewhere turn a church's own boast around ("You say, 'I am rich,'" 3:17).

p: The Greek Old Testament read Psalm 2:9 as "shepherd," and John follows it.
b: In Psalm 2:8–9 God promises his king the nations: "You will crush them with an iron rod" (Psalm 2:9). The Hebrew tero'em, "you will break them," has the same consonants as tir'em, "you will shepherd them," and the Septuagint read it the second way. John quotes that Greek, so the Plain says "shepherd," as in 12:5; the shepherd's iron-tipped club both guards and strikes. In Revelation the words describe Jesus (12:5; 19:15), and here they are shared with his faithful people.

a: just as I myself have received it from my Father
p: English Bibles end verse 27 with this clause. The Greek editions put it in verse 28.
b: The KJV and most English Bibles end 2:27 with "even as I received of my Father," so 2:28 is only the promise of the morning star. The SBL Greek text and NA28, which this site follows, start 2:28 with that clause. The words are the same in both; only the verse number differs. "It" is the authority over the nations promised in 2:26.
orig: ὡς κἀγὼ εἴληφα παρὰ τοῦ πατρός μου

p: Venus, the bright herald of dawn. Jesus says he is the star (22:16).
b: Roman generals claimed Venus as their patron, and Roman coins linked the emperor with stars. Numbers 24:17 promises, "A star will march out of Jacob." In 22:16 Jesus calls himself "the bright Morning Star." The promise is not a prize but Jesus himself.

p: "Name" comes four times in the Sardis letter. Many English Bibles hide it with "reputation" and "people."
b: Sardis has "a name" for being alive (3:1). It has "a few names" who have kept their clothes clean (3:4), using "names" for people, as in Acts 1:15. The winner's "name" will never be erased, and Jesus will declare his "name" before the Father (3:5). The letter plays a name that is only a reputation against a name written in the book of life. Translations that say "reputation" and "a few people" are correct in sense but lose the thread.

a: You have a name for being alive, but you are dead
p: A city living on its past glory, twice captured because no one was watching.
b: Sardis's citadel was thought impossible to capture. Yet it fell to Cyrus in 547 BC and to Antiochus III in 214 BC when soldiers climbed the cliffs at night and found the walls unguarded. "Be on the watch" and "I will come like a thief" hit home.

a: I will come like a thief
p: Jesus’s own picture for a coming no one expects.
b: Jesus: "if the master of the house had known during which watch of the night the thief would come, he would have stayed awake" (Matthew 24:43). Paul: "the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2). Revelation repeats it at Armageddon (16:15). Here it may mean a coming in judgment on one church, not only the final return.

p: Cities kept rolls of citizens. Names could be struck off.
b: Greek cities kept registers of citizens, and a convicted person's name could be erased. Moses asks God to "wipe me out, please, from your book that you have written" (Exodus 32:32–33). Jesus promises the opposite: "I will never erase." The Greek uses a strong double negative.

a: I will declare his name before my Father
p: An echo of Jesus’s saying in the Gospels about declaring for him in public.
b: Jesus said: "everyone who openly declares for me in front of people, I too will declare for that person in front of my Father in heaven" (Matthew 10:32). In Luke 12:8 the same saying ends "in front of God's angels" (Luke 12:8). Revelation joins both forms: "before my Father and before his angels." In Sardis, where it was easier to fit in quietly, the promise is for those who did not hide whose they were.

p: From Isaiah 22, where a steward receives the palace keys.
b: Isaiah 22:22: "I will lay the key of David's house on his shoulder. When he opens, no one will shut; when he shuts, no one will open." Eliakim became the king's chief steward. Jesus holds that authority over who enters the kingdom, just as the "synagogue of Satan" was trying to shut the door on the believers.

a: who say they are Jews and are not
t: "They will bow down at your feet"
p: A reversal of Isaiah, where the nations bow to Israel.
b: Isaiah 60:14 says those who looked down on Zion "will bow at the soles of your feet," and Isaiah 49:23 says kings will bow to her and lick the dust of her feet. Here the promise is turned around: the local synagogue opponents will acknowledge the (largely Gentile) church. Church-and-Israel views read this differently: as a temporary local conflict (most), as the church inheriting Israel's promises (replacement views), or as Gentiles grafted into Israel (Romans 11).

a: keep you from the hour of testing
p: The key verse for a pre-tribulation rapture, and a famous debate.
b: The Greek is tērēsō ek, "I will keep out of." Pre-tribulation readers say this means removal before the tribulation. Others note that John 17:15 uses the same words, "keep them safe from the evil one," where Jesus explicitly says he is not asking that they be taken out of the world. The reason given is also debated: "the word of my endurance" may mean Jesus's word calling for endurance, or the message about his own endurance, which they share (Beale, Aune); the Plain keeps the Greek open. So it can mean protection within. Preterists read it as a promise to the Philadelphia church about a coming crisis in their own time.

p: Philadelphia had been shaken by earthquakes. Pillars were often left standing.
b: After the great earthquake of AD 17 Philadelphians feared aftershocks and many lived outside the walls. In ruined cities the pillars are often what stands. Leading citizens were honored with inscribed pillars in temples. Jesus promises a permanent place, with a new name written on it.

p: From Isaiah 65:16, "the God of Amen."
b: Isaiah 65:16 literally speaks of "the God of Amen," usually translated "the God of truth." The same passage promises new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17). Jesus is God's "Yes," the one in whom God's promises come true (2 Corinthians 1:20).

p: Archē can mean the first in a series, the origin of something, or its ruler. A famous debate.
b: Archē can mean "beginning" (KJV, ESV), "origin, source" (NRSV, BSB "Originator") or "ruler" (NIV). Arius in the 300s, and Jehovah's Witnesses today, read it as "the first thing God created." Most interpreters answer that Revelation gives the same word to God: "the Beginning and the End" (21:6; 22:13), where it cannot mean the first creature. The closest parallel, Colossians 1:15–18, also written to the Lycus Valley churches near Laodicea, calls Christ "the beginning" and says all things were created in him. So most read "the source" or "the ruler" of creation. The Plain keeps "beginning" so the reader can see the Greek's range.
orig: ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κτίσεως τοῦ θεοῦ (hē archē tēs ktiseōs tou theou)

t: Lukewarm does not mean "better cold than lukewarm"
p: Zeal versus indifference, useless water, or a drink spat out? Three readings, none praising hostility.
b: There are three main readings. (1) The traditional one: hot is zeal for God, cold is open rejection, and lukewarm is indifference, the worst of the three. Its strong form, "God would rather you were against him," is a common mistake, since nothing here praises hostility. (2) The local-water reading (M. J. S. Rudwick and E. M. B. Green, Expository Times, 1958; followed by Hemer and others): hot springs at nearby Hierapolis were good for healing, Colossae may have had cool, fresh water (the evidence is thin), and Laodicea's water came by aqueduct, tepid and full of minerals. Hot and cold are both good; lukewarm means useless. (3) Craig Koester doubts the local link and points to dining customs: hosts served drinks either hot or chilled, and a lukewarm drink was spat out. On (2) and (3), the church is not half-hearted so much as useless to its Lord.
orig: ψυχρός (psychros, cold), ζεστός (zestos, hot), χλιαρός (chliaros, lukewarm)

t: Laodicea’s gold, wool and eye salve
p: Three things Laodicea was proud of: banks, black wool, and a medical school.
b: Laodicea was a banking city, rich enough to rebuild without Rome's help (see the note on 3:17). It was famous for glossy black wool and had a medical school associated with a "Phrygian powder" used for eyes. Jesus offers better gold, white clothes, and real sight.

p: From Proverbs 3:12, also quoted in Hebrews 12:6.
b: Proverbs 3:12: "whoever the LORD loves, he rebukes, / the way a father treats the son he takes pleasure in." Hebrews 12:5–6 quotes the same proverb to a church under pressure. Here Jesus speaks it to the harshest-rebuked church of the seven, so even "I am going to vomit you out" (3:16) comes from love, not rejection. The Greek paideuō is a father's training of a child.

a: I am standing at the door, knocking
t: A door to the heart, or to the church?
p: Spoken to a church, it is an invitation to a meal.
b: This is often used to invite one person to faith, and that is a fair application. In context Jesus speaks to a whole church that has shut him out. The image echoes Song of Songs 5:2 ("my beloved is knocking"), and "eat with" points to the Lord's Supper and the wedding supper (19:9). Some futurists read it of the last church age.

p: Some see the church raptured here. The words are spoken to John.
b: Pre-tribulation readers note that the word "church" is not used again until 22:16 and see 4:1 as a picture of the church caught up before the tribulation. Others point out that the call is to John alone, who is "in the Spirit" (4:2), and that the same words are spoken to the two witnesses in 11:12.

p: Ezekiel saw it around the throne, and it recalls God’s promise after the flood.
b: In Ezekiel 1:28 the brightness around God's throne looks like a bow in the clouds on a day of rain. In Genesis 9:13–16 the bow is a sign of God's promise never again to destroy the earth by flood. Judgment is about to come from this throne, but mercy surrounds it.

p: Twelve tribes plus twelve apostles? Angels? Priestly leaders? The raptured church?
b: Popular readings: the people of God of both covenants (12 tribes + 12 apostles, matching the city's gates and foundations in 21:12–14); the 24 divisions of priests in 1 Chronicles 24; a council of angels; or, for many dispensationalists (Walvoord), the church already raptured, crowned and seated in heaven before the tribulation (see the note on 4:1). Their white clothes and crowns are promised to overcomers (3:5; 2:10).

p: KJV "four beasts," but the Greek means "living ones."
b: The KJV calls the creatures by God's throne "four beasts." The Greek zōa means "living ones." The monster of chapter 13 is a different word, thērion. In 1611 "beast" meant any animal, so the KJV was not wrong for its day. Today it puts God's worshipers and God's enemies under one label. NKJV, ESV, NIV and NASB all say "living creatures."

p: The calm "waters above" the sky, laid at God’s feet like a pavement.
b: Ancient people pictured waters above the sky (Genesis 1:7; Psalm 148:4), and the Bible puts God's throne above them. At Sinai the elders saw under God's feet "what looked like a floor of blue lapis stone" (Exodus 24:10), and Ezekiel saw a shining, crystal-like expanse above the creatures' heads (Ezekiel 1:22). Solomon's temple had a huge bronze basin called "the Sea" (1 Kings 7:23). In Revelation the sea is often the home of chaos and the beast (13:1), and here it lies still before God. In 15:2 it is "mixed with fire," and the winners stand beside it, and in the new creation there is no more sea (21:1).

a: The first living creature looked like a lion
p: The strongest of the wild animals, tame animals, birds, and all creatures.
b: A Jewish saying put it this way: the mightiest among birds is the eagle, among tame animals the ox, among wild animals the lion, and over them all is the human (Midrash Rabbah on Exodus 15:1). The creatures represent all creation worshiping God. Irenaeus (about AD 180) matched them to the four Gospels, the start of a long Christian art tradition.

p: The six-winged seraphim sang this in Isaiah 6.
b: Isaiah 6:2–3: seraphim with six wings call to each other, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Armies." John combines Isaiah's seraphim with Ezekiel's four-faced creatures (Ezekiel 1:5–10; 10:14). This song became the "Sanctus" in Christian worship.

a: You are worthy, our Lord and God
p: Domitian liked to be called "our lord and god." Here the title goes to the Creator.
b: The Roman historian Suetonius says Domitian had letters issued in the name of "our lord and god" (dominus et deus noster, Domitian 13). Crowds in the arena hailed emperors with "Worthy!" (Latin dignus, Greek axios). The elders lay their crowns down, as client kings did before the emperor.

p: Roman wills were sealed by seven witnesses and opened only at the right time.
b: Roman law required one form of will to be sealed by seven witnesses. Legal deeds were often written inside and summarized on the outside. Ezekiel's scroll was written on the front and on the back (Ezekiel 2:9–10), and Daniel was told to keep his words sealed until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4). Manuscripts differ on "on the back," and some scholars read "written inside, and sealed on the back"; see the variant on this verse.

a: the Lion from the tribe of Judah
t: John hears "Lion" and sees a Lamb
p: The book’s key move: power redefined as sacrifice.
b: The elder announces a Lion (Genesis 49:9) and the Root of David (Isaiah 11:1, 10), Israel's warrior-messiah. John looks and sees a slaughtered Lamb. Bauckham calls this the key to the book: the Messiah wins by dying. Bauckham also points out that the same hear-then-see pattern returns in 7:4–9, where John hears 144,000 from Israel's tribes and sees a crowd no one could count (The Climax of Prophecy, chapter 7). My own small addition: in both places what John hears is the form of Israel's promise, and what he sees is the way it comes true, so the pattern may be meant as a key for reading other paired scenes in the book.

p: Arnion, "lamb," "slaughtered" like a sacrifice, yet standing. Why the Plain says "he."
b: Arnion has the form of a diminutive, "little lamb," but by John's time it had mostly lost that force and meant simply "lamb" (John 21:15 uses it for Peter's flock). Esphagmenon means "slaughtered," a sacrifice word, stronger than "slain." Arnion is neuter, "it," but in 5:6 John goes on with a masculine word, "having" (echōn), as if the Lamb is plainly a person; so the Plain says "he." The Lamb stands alive yet still bears the marks. It is the book's main name for Jesus: 29 uses, 28 of them for Christ. The one other use is the land beast, which has horns "like a lamb" (13:11).

p: Complete power and complete knowledge.
b: Horns stand for power and kingship (Daniel 7:24; Psalm 18:2). The seven eyes are the seven Spirits of God, sent out into the whole earth, an image from Zechariah 4:10, where seven lamps are the LORD's eyes roaming over all the earth. The Lamb is weak-looking and all-powerful at once.

p: Psalm 141:2: "Let my prayer be set up as incense in front of you."
b: Prayer rising like incense comes from Psalm 141:2. These bowls return in 8:3–5, where the prayers are mixed with fire and thrown to the earth, and the trumpets begin. The world's judgment is God's answer to his people's prayers.

a: every tribe and language and people and nation
p: Seven times the book lists all humanity in four parts.
b: The fourfold formula (in varying order) appears at 5:9; 7:9; 10:11; 11:9; 13:7; 14:6; 17:15: seven times four. It may echo Genesis 10, where the peoples spread out, each with its own language, "by their clans, in their nations" (Genesis 10:5; compare Genesis 10:20, 31). The Lamb's people undo Babel.

p: In Daniel 7:10 myriads upon myriads stand before the Ancient of Days.
b: The Greek myriades myriadōn is the largest number the language could easily say. It is taken directly from Daniel 7:10, where it surrounds the Ancient of Days at the judgment. A picture of a number beyond counting, not a census.

p: Christ, the gospel, a false Christ, or a conquering empire?
b: Christ or the gospel (Irenaeus, many historicists), because Christ rides a white horse in 19:11. A false Christ (many futurists), because Jesus warned that deceivers come first (Matthew 24:4–5). Conquest itself, the first of four disasters. The bow suggests the Parthians, the mounted archers Rome feared.

a: A quart of wheat for a denarius
t: "A measure of wheat for a penny"
p: Not cheap: a full day’s pay for one person’s bread.
b: A dēnarion was a full day's pay for a worker (Matthew 20:2). A choinix, about a quart, was one person's daily ration. So the voice announces a whole day's wage for one person's bread: famine prices, roughly ten times normal by the estimates commentators draw from grain prices recorded elsewhere in the empire. A worker could feed himself but not his family. The KJV's "penny" makes it sound cheap. The Plain keeps the coin's name, "denarius," in both halves of the saying, as the Greek does.

a: leave the oil and the wine unharmed
p: About AD 92 Domitian ordered vineyards cut back, then backed down.
b: Suetonius (Domitian 7, 14) says Domitian, during a grain shortage, ordered half the vineyards in the provinces destroyed, but cancelled the order after protests, possibly from Asia. Whether or not John had this in mind, the picture is of a famine where basic grain is scarce while luxury goods continue.

p: Chlōros: the gray-green color of a corpse.
b: Chlōros (the root of "chlorophyll") means pale green, the gray-green of a corpse. Revelation uses the same word for green grass in 8:7 and 9:4.

a: with the sword, with hunger, with disease, and by the wild animals
p: Ezekiel 14:21 names the same four: sword, famine, wild animals and plague.
b: The fourth rider's list is borrowed from Ezekiel 14:21, where God sends four harmful judgments on Jerusalem: the sword, famine, wild animals and plague. It also follows the covenant curses of Leviticus 26:21–26. The horsemen are not random disasters; they are the old covenant warnings coming to pass.

p: Sacrificial blood was poured at the base of the altar.
b: In the temple, the blood of a sacrifice was poured out at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7). The martyrs are pictured as sacrifices, and the Greek word for them, "slaughtered" (esphagmenōn), is the word used for the Lamb in 5:6, 9 and 12: they share his death. Paul calls his coming death being "poured out like a drink offering" (2 Timothy 4:6).

p: The cry of the psalms of lament.
b: "How long?" is the prayer of Psalm 13:1–2, Psalm 79:5–10, Psalm 94:3 and Zechariah 1:12. Psalm 79:10 asks God to let the nations see "the vengeance for your servants' blood that was spilled." The rest of the book is the answer to this question, beginning with the angel's oath, "There will be no more waiting" (10:6).

a: all of the moon became like blood
p: Joel says the sun will turn dark and the moon to blood before the day of the LORD.
b: The cosmic signs come from Joel 2:31, Isaiah 13:10 and Isaiah 34:4 (the sky rolled up like a scroll). In Isaiah these signs announce the fall of Babylon and Edom, real historical judgments, described in world-ending language. Futurists expect literal events; preterists and idealists read prophetic "collapse of the world order" language. Some today connect "blood moons" (lunar eclipses) to these verses.

p: Hosea 10:8, and Jesus’s words on the way to the cross.
b: In Hosea 10:8 the people of Israel, facing judgment, beg the mountains to cover them and the hills to fall on them. Jesus uses the words for the women of Jerusalem: they will start "telling the mountains, 'Fall on us,' and the hills, 'Cover us'" (Luke 23:30), warning of the city's coming destruction. Preterists see that link as support for a first-century focus.

p: A deliberately strange phrase. Lambs are not angry.
b: No ancient reader would expect anger from a lamb. My reading: the phrase holds together two things the book will not separate. The judge is the one who was slaughtered for the people now hiding. His anger is the anger of rejected love, not of a tyrant. This fits 14:10, where the torment happens "in front of the Lamb."

p: A figure of speech for the whole world, still used today.
b: Isaiah 11:12 speaks of gathering Israel's scattered people "from the earth's four corners" too. Ancient writers used it as we use "the four corners of the globe." The four winds are agents of judgment (Jeremiah 49:36; Zechariah 6:5).

p: Ezekiel 9: a mark on those who grieve over sin protected them.
b: In Ezekiel 9:4–6 a man in linen marks the foreheads of the faithful in Jerusalem before the city's judgment. The Hebrew mark is the letter tav, which in old script looked like an X or a cross. The beast's mark in chapter 13 is a counterfeit of this seal.

p: Jewish believers, the whole church, or a special group?
b: Ethnic Israel: Jewish believers in the end times (many futurists). The whole people of God, pictured as Israel's army (many amillennialists), since the crowd John sees next is the same group. Jewish Christians of the first century (some preterists). A literal number of an elite group (Jehovah's Witnesses).

a: Out of the tribe of Judah
p: Judah first, Dan and Ephraim missing.
b: There are about 20 tribal lists in the Old Testament, and this one matches none. Judah, the tribe of the Messiah, comes first instead of Reuben. Dan is missing; Irenaeus thought the antichrist would come from Dan (Jeremiah 8:16; Genesis 49:17), and Dan was linked to idolatry (Judges 18; 1 Kings 12:29). Ephraim is absent but Joseph is named. Levi, usually left out of military lists, is included.

a: a crowd so large that no one could count it
t: The promise to Abraham, counted and uncountable
p: 144,000 is what John hears. What he sees is Abraham’s uncountable family.
b: God told Abraham to "number the stars, if you can number them... So will your offspring be" (Genesis 15:5) and "too many to count" (Genesis 16:10; 32:12). The census in 7:4–8 is a military muster like Numbers 1. My view, following Bauckham: the crowd is the same group as the 144,000, seen as it truly is, Abraham's promise fulfilled through every nation, just as John heard "Lion" and saw "Lamb" in chapter 5.

p: Waved at the Feast of Tabernacles and at victories.
b: Palm branches were used at the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:40), at the victory celebrations of the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7), and at Jesus's entry into Jerusalem (John 12:13). 7:15 says God will "spread his tent over them," another Tabernacles echo.

p: One future seven-year period, or the suffering of the whole church age?
b: The Greek has the article: "the great tribulation," as in Daniel 12:1 and Matthew 24:21. Futurists see a specific future period, and this crowd as people saved during it. Preterists see the war of AD 66–70 and the persecutions of the time. Idealists note John says he already shares "the suffering" (1:9) with his readers, and that the Greek is present tense: these are "the ones who are coming out" (hoi erchomenoi), a stream still arriving, not a group that came out once.

a: washed their robes and made them white in the blood
p: A paradox: red blood makes white robes.
b: The image draws on Exodus 19:10, 14, where the people wash their clothes before meeting God at Sinai, and on Isaiah 1:18, where sins red as scarlet are made white as snow. The blessing in 22:14 repeats it.

a: They will never go hungry again
p: 7:16–17 quotes Isaiah 49:10, but gives the shepherd’s role to the Lamb.
b: Isaiah 49:10 promises exiles coming home that they will not go hungry or thirsty and that sun and scorching wind will not strike them, "for the one who pities them will lead them / and guide them to springs of water" (Isaiah 49:10). John follows the Greek of Isaiah closely, but the one who leads is now "the Lamb in the middle of the throne." The one who was led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7) has become the shepherd (compare Ezekiel 34:23; Psalm 23).

a: God will wipe every tear from their eyes
p: Isaiah 25:8: "The Lord GOD will wipe the tears off every face."
b: Isaiah 25:6–8 describes a feast for all peoples on God's mountain, where death is swallowed up forever and tears are wiped away. Revelation uses this promise here and again in 21:4.

a: silence in heaven for about half an hour
p: Heaven falls silent before the incense and the prayers. How long did the incense offering take?
b: Habakkuk 2:20 and Zephaniah 1:7 call for silence before the LORD's judgment. At the incense hour the people stood outside the temple praying (Luke 1:10). The Talmud says companies of angels sing by night and keep silent by day, for the honor of Israel (Hagigah 12b); other rabbinic texts picture heaven's praise waiting on Israel's. Commentators from R. H. Charles to Richard Bauckham have tied the silence to the incense offering and the prayers of 8:3–4, so that part is not new. My own guess, which no ancient source supports directly, is that "half an hour" is meant as the time the evening incense offering took.

p: Ezekiel 10: coals from between the cherubim scattered over Jerusalem.
b: In Ezekiel 10:2 a man in linen fills his hands with burning coals from among the cherubim and scatters them over the city. The prayers of 6:10 rise, and the answer comes down as fire.

a: Hail and fire came, mixed with blood
p: The trumpets copy the plagues of Exodus.
b: Hail and fire (Exodus 9:23–25), water to blood (Exodus 7:20), darkness (Exodus 10:21), locusts (Exodus 10:12–15). The trumpets and bowls retell the Exodus on a world scale, with the beast's kingdom as Egypt and the church as Israel leaving it.

p: Limited judgment: a warning, not yet the end.
b: Trumpet judgments strike "a third" again and again (12 times in chapter 8). The bowls later strike everything. The partial strikes are warnings that leave room to repent, which 9:20–21 says people refused to do. Compare Ezekiel 5:2, 12, where Jerusalem's people are divided into thirds.

a: a great burning mountain was thrown into the sea
p: Vesuvius erupted in AD 79. Some modern scholars hear an echo of it here.
b: Some modern scholars connect the burning mountain with the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, which buried Pompeii. No ancient reader is known to have linked this verse with Vesuvius, but the Jewish Sibylline Oracles (4.130–136) do treat the eruption as God's punishment of Rome. In Jeremiah 51:25 God tells Babylon, "I will ... turn you into a mountain of burning" (Jeremiah 51:25). Others read the mountain as a fallen kingdom, since mountains often stand for kingdoms in prophecy.
l: Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD
Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD

p: A bitter plant, used by the prophets for judgment.
b: In Jeremiah 9:15 God warns that he will feed his unfaithful people wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink. Here the star passes its own name to the water: "a third of the waters turned into wormwood." Many people linked this verse to Chernobyl (1986), because the Ukrainian word names a related plant (mugwort).

p: Satan, a fallen angel, or simply an angel sent down?
b: The Greek is a perfect tense, "had fallen," which suggests the star fell before John saw it. Isaiah 14:12 describes the fall of the "morning star." Jesus says, "I was watching Satan fall like lightning out of heaven" (Luke 10:18). Others note that 20:1 has a good angel holding the same key, and read this star as an angel sent on a mission.

p: Joel 2 describes an invading army as locusts that look like horses.
b: Joel 1–2 pictures a locust swarm that looks like horses, has a lion's teeth, and sounds like chariots racing over the hilltops. Joel used a real locust plague to picture an invading army and the Day of the LORD. Readers have seen in these locusts Muslim armies (historicists), modern attack helicopters (some futurists), Roman armies (preterists), or demonic torment (idealists).

p: The life span of a locust, or the length of the locust season.
b: Locusts typically live about five months, and the dry season when they swarm (May to September) is about that long. Some preterists, as Gregg's survey of the views reports, connect it to the five months of Gessius Florus's violence in AD 66, or to the five months of the Roman siege of Jerusalem in AD 70.

p: Hebrew "Destruction," Greek "Destroyer." A jab at Apollo?
b: Abaddon is a Hebrew word for the place of destruction (Job 26:6; Proverbs 15:11). The Greek name Apollyōn sounds like Apollo, whose symbols included the locust. Emperors such as Nero and Domitian liked to be associated with Apollo. Many scholars think John is mocking the emperor's patron god. John gives the names but does not translate them; the meaning "Destroyer" is the reader's to hear.

p: The eastern border of Rome, and beyond it the feared Parthians.
b: The Euphrates was the boundary between the Roman Empire and the Parthian Empire. Parthian horse-archers could shoot backward while riding, which may explain power "in their tails" (9:19). Rumors that Nero would return leading a Parthian army spread in the decades after his death.

a: The cavalry armies numbered two hundred million
p: A literal army from Asia, or a number meaning "beyond counting"?
b: The Greek is literally "double myriads of myriads," twice the myriads of myriads around the throne in 5:11 (a myriad is ten thousand). Some futurists have pointed to China, which once claimed a militia of 200 million. Most others read a demonic host too big for any earthly army. Yet John adds that he "heard how many there were": unlike the crowd of 7:9, this host is counted. The Byzantine manuscripts read simply "myriads of myriads" (see the variant).

a: did not even repent of what their hands had made
p: The prophets’ mockery of idols, and Pharaoh’s hard heart.
b: The list of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood idols that cannot see, hear, or walk comes from Daniel 5:23 and Psalm 115:4–7. Like Pharaoh after each plague (Exodus 8:15), people refuse to repent. Judgment in Revelation is aimed at repentance, which is why its failure is noted.

p: The root of "pharmacy," but here it means magic: potions, poisons and spells.
b: The text the Plain follows has pharmaka, the potions, poisons and charms of magic. The Byzantine text, followed by the KJV ("sorceries"), has the related word pharmakeia, "sorcery," the word used in 18:23, where Babylon deceives the nations by her sorcery (see the variant). Some modern preachers read either word as drug use or even the medical industry. In ancient usage both are about magic, often the harmful kind: love potions, curses and poisons.

p: His face shines like the sun, as Jesus’s face does in 1:16.
b: The cloud recalls Jesus coming with the clouds (1:7), the rainbow the throne of 4:3, the face like the sun Jesus in 1:16, and the feet of fire the glowing feet of 1:15. Some take him to be Christ, or the Angel of the LORD, among them many older historicists and the Reformed commentator G. K. Beale. Most note he is called "another angel," swears by God rather than by himself, and resembles the angel of Daniel 10–12.

a: Keep under seal what the seven thunders said
p: The one secret in an unsealed book.
b: Some think the thunders were a series of judgments God decided to skip, in mercy (Bauckham). Others take it as a warning to humble interpreters: not everything is revealed (Deuteronomy 29:29). Psalm 29 names "the LORD's voice" seven times, and it thunders.

a: There will be no more waiting
p: KJV "time no longer" is not about the end of time.
b: KJV: "that there should be time no longer." This has often been preached as "time itself will end and eternity begins." In context the angel is answering the martyrs' cry, "How long?" (6:10). Chronos here means a waiting period, and most modern translations render the line as "no more delay." The Plain says "There will be no more waiting." The scene answers Daniel 12:7, where an angel swears how long the waiting will be.

a: the mystery of God is finished
t: The mystery announced to the prophets
p: Amos 3:7: the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets.
b: The angel's words echo Amos 3:7, where the Hebrew says the Lord GOD does nothing unless he has revealed his secret counsel to his servants the prophets, and Daniel 12:7. In the New Testament "mystery" means God's plan once hidden and now revealed: Christ, and Gentiles joined with Israel (Ephesians 3:3–6; Romans 16:25–26).

t: "Is finished": a past tense for the future
p: The Greek uses a past tense for something still to come, as if it were already done.
b: The verb is an aorist, a past tense: literally "and the mystery of God was finished." Most translations say "will be finished," which is the sense, since the seventh trumpet has not yet sounded. But John speaks as the prophets often did, of a future act of God as though it had already happened. The same verb (teleō) is Jesus's last word on the cross, "It is finished" (John 19:30).

t: "Told the good news": the word behind "gospel"
p: God "gospeled" his plan to the prophets. Even the end, judgment included, is called good news.
b: Euangelizō is the verb behind the noun euangelion, "good news," which English Bibles call "the gospel." Most translations say God "announced" or "declared" his mystery to the prophets, which hides the word. In the Greek of Isaiah it is the herald's word, "the one who brings good news" (Isaiah 52:7; compare Isaiah 40:9). John uses it again for the angel with "eternal good news" (14:6). That God's final plan, judgment and all, is called good news is one of the book's quiet surprises: the end is the coming of God's kingdom (11:15).

p: Ezekiel ate a scroll that tasted like honey.
b: In Ezekiel 3:1–3 God tells Ezekiel to eat a scroll and then go and speak to Israel, and in his mouth it was sweet like honey. Yet that scroll was written front and back with laments, moaning and wailing (Ezekiel 2:10). God's word is sweet to receive and painful to carry. John's scroll turns his stomach bitter, the same verb used when the waters were "made bitter" by Wormwood (8:11).

p: The little Greek word epi can mean about, against, or before. Each gives the commission a different tone.
b: With the dative, epi can mean "about, concerning," "against" (as in the prophets' oracles against the nations, Jeremiah 46–51; Ezekiel 25–32), or "to, before" (the nations as his audience). Most translations say "about." Commentators, including Aune and Beale, weigh the options: "against" fits the judgments that follow; "about" or "to" fits the book's hope that the nations will turn to God (11:13; 15:4). The Plain says "about," the widest of the three.

p: Herod’s temple before AD 70, a future rebuilt temple, or the church?
b: Preterists: the temple still stood when John wrote, so this was written before AD 70 and describes the siege. Futurists: a rebuilt third temple during the tribulation. Idealists and many others: the church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16), protected inwardly while its outer life is trampled. Measuring signals protection, as in Ezekiel 40–42 and Zechariah 2:1–5.

p: Revelation names 3½ years in several ways, but never "seven years."
b: Revelation names a 3½-year period in several ways: 42 months, 1,260 days, and "a time, times and half a time." The seven-year tribulation comes from joining these to the "one week" of Daniel 9:27. That can be argued, but the number seven is built from Daniel, not stated in Revelation.
orig: μῆνας τεσσεράκοντα δύο (42 months); ἡμέρας χιλίας διακοσίας ἑξήκοντα (1,260 days)

a: They will trample the holy city
p: Jesus: "Jerusalem will be trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled."
b: Luke 21:24 uses the same words. Daniel 8:13 also speaks of the sanctuary being trampled. Preterists read the Roman siege; futurists a future occupation; idealists the church's suffering in the world.

a: the two olive trees and the two lampstands
p: In Zechariah 4 the two olive trees are a governor and a priest: in Hebrew, "the two sons of oil."
b: In Zechariah 4:3, 11–14 two olive trees feed oil to a lampstand. The angel explains them with a Hebrew idiom: they are "the two sons of the fresh oil who stand by the Lord of all the earth." Most English Bibles turn "sons of oil" into "anointed ones," but the word is yitshar, fresh olive oil, not the usual word for anointing oil, so some scholars read "the two who supply the oil" rather than "the two anointed." They are probably Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest. Revelation keeps Zechariah's title for God, "the Lord of the earth." Its two witnesses are also two lampstands, which in 1:20 stand for churches.

p: One shuts the sky like Elijah, the other turns water to blood like Moses.
b: Elijah stopped the rain (1 Kings 17:1) and called down fire (2 Kings 1:10). Moses turned water to blood (Exodus 7:20). Malachi 4:5 promised Elijah's return, and Moses and Elijah appear with Jesus at the transfiguration (Mark 9:4).

p: "Where their Lord was crucified" sounds like Jerusalem. But "the great city" is Babylon everywhere else.
b: Preterists read Jerusalem: "where their Lord too was crucified." Others note that "the great city" is always Babylon later (16:19; 17:18; 18:10) and that John says it is called Sodom and Egypt "symbolically" (literally "spiritually"). On that reading it is the world's city, which crucified Jesus through Rome's governor.

p: The Greek says "their corpse," singular, then "their corpses," plural.
b: In 11:8 and the start of 11:9 the Greek has the singular, "their corpse," and then switches to the plural, "their corpses." Most translations smooth this into "their bodies." The singular may be a Hebrew-style way of speaking of something each of them has, but readers who see the two witnesses as one witnessing church take it as a hint that the two are one.
orig: τὸ πτῶμα αὐτῶν (to ptōma autōn), singular

p: Esther ends with feasting and sending gifts after enemies are defeated. Here the world feasts over God’s prophets.
b: At Purim the Jews kept "a day for sending portions of food to one another" (Esther 9:19), after their enemies were defeated (Esther 9:19–22). Beale and others already note the allusion. Revelation's words are not the same as the Greek of Esther, but the scene matches: the world rejoices, celebrates and sends gifts, this time over the death of God's prophets. My own suggestion goes one step further: the scene is a deliberate inversion of Purim, and as in Esther, the celebration is overturned in a moment (11:11).

a: a breath of life from God went into them
p: In Ezekiel 37 breath enters the dead, and they stand on their feet.
b: In Ezekiel 37:10 breath comes into the slain, and they come to life and stand on their feet, a vast army. Revelation uses the same words for the two witnesses. Ezekiel's vision was about Israel restored from exile; John applies it to God's witnesses raised after their defeat. The Greek pneuma, like the Hebrew ruach, means both "breath" and "spirit."

p: The same words as 4:1. Some see a mid-tribulation rapture here.
b: Mid-tribulation readers see the church (pictured by the witnesses) raised and caught up halfway through, before the seventh trumpet, linking it to Paul's "last trumpet" (1 Corinthians 15:52). Others see a vindication scene modeled on Jesus's own resurrection and ascension.

t: "Names of people" and a city that gives glory
p: Literally "names of people, seven thousand." And for once, the survivors give glory to God.
b: The Greek counts the dead as "names of people," a Hebrew-style way of saying "persons" (compare Acts 1:15, literally "a crowd of names"). Seven thousand is the number God kept faithful in Elijah's day (1 Kings 19:18). Then "the rest were filled with fear and gave glory to the God of heaven." After the trumpets, people did not repent (9:20–21); after the witnesses' death and rising, they do. Bauckham argues that this is the book's picture of the nations turning to God through the church's faithful witness; others read it as fear without true repentance.
orig: ὀνόματα ἀνθρώπων χιλιάδες ἑπτά (onomata anthrōpōn chiliades hepta)

p: The Greek christos translates the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed." Here it is Psalm 2’s title, "his anointed."
b: Christos is the Greek word for the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one," which gives us "Messiah." Elsewhere the Plain uses "Christ" as part of Jesus's name ("Jesus Christ," 1:1). Here it is a title with "his": God's anointed king. The phrase comes from Psalm 2, where the rulers set themselves "against the LORD and against his anointed one" (Psalm 2:2). The church in Acts 4:26 reads that psalm the same way. At the seventh trumpet the psalm is answered: the world's kingdom now belongs to the Lord and his Messiah. The same title returns at 12:10.
orig: τοῦ χριστοῦ αὐτοῦ (tou christou autou), "his anointed"

p: Psalm 2 and Psalm 99 stand behind the elders’ song.
b: "Why do the nations gather in an uproar?" asks Psalm 2:1, before God installs his king. The Greek of Psalm 99:1 (98:1 in the Septuagint) begins, "The Lord has become king; let the peoples be angry," the same pair of words as 11:17–18: God takes up his reign, and the nations are furious. The Plain keeps the wordplay of the Greek: the nations' fury (ōrgisthēsan) meets God's fury (orgē).

p: Lost with the Babylonian destruction of the temple, or earlier. Here it is seen in heaven.
b: The ark disappears from the record by the time Babylon destroyed Solomon's temple in 587/586 BC; many think it was lost or taken then, some that it was gone earlier. 2 Maccabees 2:4–8 says Jeremiah hid it in a cave until God gathers his people again. Revelation's answer: the true ark was always in heaven. Various groups have claimed to have it, including the Ethiopian Orthodox Church in Aksum. Catholic and Orthodox readers pair this verse with the woman of 12:1: the liturgy of the Assumption reads them together, and the Catechism calls Mary "the ark of the covenant" (Catechism 2676). See the card on the woman in chapter 12.

a: a woman wrapped in the sun
p: Israel, Mary, the church, or all three?
b: Israel: the sun, moon and twelve stars come from Joseph's dream of his family (Genesis 37:9), and Israel "gives birth" to the Messiah (Isaiah 66:7–8; Micah 5:3). Mary: she literally bore the child (a common Catholic and Orthodox reading). The church: her other children are believers (12:17). Many readers see the faithful people of God across both covenants.

p: Goddesses were pictured crowned with stars. So was the European flag.
b: Goddesses were honored as queens of heaven. The clearest parallel is Isis: the Latin novelist Apuleius describes her appearing with a disk like the moon on her brow and a dark cloak sprinkled with glittering stars and a half moon (Metamorphoses 11.3–4, second century AD). John's woman is the true queen-mother. The circle of twelve gold stars on the European flag (1955) was partly inspired, by its designer's later account, by images of Mary based on this verse; the Council of Europe's official explanation says only that twelve stands for completeness and unity.

a: a great fiery-red dragon with seven heads
p: Canaanite texts describe Litan, "the mighty one with seven heads."
b: At Ugarit (about 1300 BC) Baal defeats Litan, "the twisting serpent, the mighty one with seven heads." The Old Testament calls this monster Leviathan and says God crushed its heads (Psalm 74:13–14; Isaiah 27:1). Babylon's Tiamat and Greek Typhon are similar chaos monsters.

t: A third of the angels fell?
p: A popular belief, but the text may mean something else.
b: Many Christians believe a third of the angels followed Satan in a rebellion before creation, based on this verse. They also point to 12:7–9, where the dragon has "his angels," who are thrown down with him, and many commentators (futurist and some idealist) do read the stars of 12:4 as those angels. On the other side, the verse is placed at the birth of Christ, and it echoes Daniel 8:10, where a horn (Antiochus) throws down some of the stars, meaning God's people. The idea of a pre-creation fall comes more from later tradition (and Milton's Paradise Lost) than from this text.

t: Revelation never uses "rapture" for the church
p: The book’s only "rapture" (harpazō) is Jesus’s own ascension.
b: "Rapture" comes from the Latin of 1 Thessalonians 4:17 (rapiemur, "we will be caught up"). Revelation uses harpazō only once, for the male child, Jesus, "snatched up to God and to his throne" (12:5). Pre-tribulation readers find the church's rapture implied at 4:1, "Come up here." Those words are spoken to John alone. The same words are spoken again in 11:12, to the two witnesses after they rise from the dead.

a: shepherd all the nations with an iron rod
t: The shepherd with the iron rod
p: Psalm 2:9 in its Greek form, already given to the faithful in 2:27.
b: The line is Psalm 2:9, the coronation psalm of God's anointed king, as the Greek Old Testament reads it: "you will shepherd them" (poimaineis). The Hebrew, read with different vowels, says "you will crush them with an iron rod" (the site's Psalm 2:9). The note at 2:27 explains the two readings. Here the promise belongs first to the child himself; 19:15 uses it again for the rider on the white horse.

a: She gave birth to a son
p: In Greek myth a dragon hunted a pregnant goddess. Ephesus told this story.
b: The dragon Python hunted the pregnant Leto to keep her from bearing Apollo. She escaped (helped by the north wind or Poseidon) and gave birth on an island. Apollo later killed Python. Ephesus claimed the birth happened nearby, and Roman emperors presented themselves as Apollo. Many scholars think John retells the myth with Jesus as the real dragon-slayer.

p: In Daniel, the great prince who stands guard over Israel.
b: In Daniel 10:13, 21 and 12:1 Michael is Israel's great prince, the one who stands over Daniel's people and rises up in a time of distress like no other. Jude 9 calls him the archangel. In Revelation the war is fought in heaven, but 12:11 says the real victory came "because of the blood of the Lamb" (12:11).

p: The dragon is the snake of Genesis 3, finally exposed.
b: Revelation names the serpent of Genesis 3 as the devil, a link the Old Testament never makes outright (compare Wisdom of Solomon 2:24, Scripture for Catholics and Orthodox, and Romans 16:20). Genesis 3:15 promised that the woman's offspring would strike the serpent on the head; chapter 12 shows a woman, a child, and the serpent. 12:17 keeps the link: "the rest of her offspring" uses sperma, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the woman's offspring in Genesis 3:15.

p: The Hebrew satan is a prosecutor, as in Job and Zechariah.
b: In Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3:1, "the satan" is the accuser in God's court. Diabolos (devil) means "slanderer." John's Greek word katēgōr is a legal term borrowed into Hebrew and Aramaic as well. After Christ's victory, the prosecutor loses his place in court (compare Romans 8:33–34).

a: They won the victory over him because of the blood of the Lamb
p: The war in heaven is won on earth, by a cross and by testimony.
b: Verses 7–9 show an angelic war; verses 10–11 reveal how it was really won: because of the Lamb's blood, because of believers' testimony, and through their refusal to love their lives (on "because of" or "by," see the word note on this verse). My reading: Michael's battle is the heavenly side of the cross, which explains why it happens right after the child is "snatched up" (12:5). Jesus links his death with Satan being "thrown out" in John 12:31–32.

a: because of the blood of the Lamb
p: With this case, dia usually gives the reason, not the tool.
b: Dia followed by the accusative case normally means "because of" or "on account of." Many English Bibles say "by the blood of the Lamb," as if the blood and the testimony were the weapons used. The grammar points first to the reason: the believers won because the Lamb had died and because they held to their testimony, even to death (Aune and Koester read it this way). "By" is still defensible, since a cause can also be a means, and the two senses meet at the cross. The Plain follows the usual meaning of the grammar.
orig: διὰ τὸ αἷμα ... διὰ τὸν λόγον (dia to haima ... dia ton logon)

a: two wings of the great eagle
p: God said he lifted Israel up "on the wings of eagles."
b: Exodus 19:4: "I lifted you up on the wings of eagles and brought you to me." Deuteronomy 32:11 pictures God as an eagle spreading its wings over its young. The woman's flight into the wilderness, where she is fed, retells Israel's Exodus and manna. Some preterists see the Jerusalem church fleeing to Pella before AD 70 (Eusebius 3.5.3).

a: a time, and times, and half a time
p: Daniel 7:25 and 12:7: three and a half "times."
b: The phrase comes from Daniel 7:25 and Daniel 12:7. Here it equals the 1,260 days of 12:6, which shows that John treats the different phrases as one period.

p: In the Exodus story, the earth swallowed Pharaoh’s army and later Korah.
b: Exodus 15:12 says of Pharaoh's army at the sea: "the earth swallowed them." Numbers 16:32: "the earth opened its mouth and swallowed" Korah's rebels. Creation itself takes the side of God's people.

t: Who are "the rest of her offspring"?
p: The church on earth, a future remnant, or (for Adventists) a last-days remnant church?
b: The woman's son is safe with God; her other children stay on earth and bear the dragon's attack. Most readers, ancient and modern, see the whole church after Christ's ascension, made up of all who keep God's commandments and hold to Jesus' testimony. Many futurists see believers, often Jewish believers, in the last three and a half years. Seventh-day Adventists read the KJV's "remnant of her seed" as the last-days remnant church: those who keep all of God's commandments, the Sabbath included, and who have "the testimony of Jesus," which 19:10 calls the spirit of prophecy. Adventist teaching sees that gift at work in the ministry of Ellen G. White, and identifies the Seventh-day Adventist Church with this remnant, while holding that God has faithful people in every church (Fundamental Beliefs 13 and 18). Other Christians do not accept that identification.

p: The testimony about Jesus, or the testimony Jesus himself gave?
b: The Greek simply says "the testimony of Jesus," and the phrase can mean two things. It can be the testimony believers give about Jesus (many translations), or the testimony Jesus himself gave as the faithful witness of 1:5, which believers hold on to and pass on (1:2, 9). Many commentators think John means both. The same question comes back at 14:12 ("the faith of Jesus") and 19:10 and 20:4. The Plain keeps the open Greek here; for Adventist readings of this verse, see the note on "the rest of her offspring."

a: a beast coming up out of the sea
p: Leopard, bear and lion, the beasts of Daniel 7, combined.
b: Daniel 7:3–7 sees four beasts rise from the sea: a lion, a bear, a leopard, and a terrible fourth beast with ten horns. John's beast combines all four, in reverse order. Daniel's beasts are kingdoms (7:17). In John's time, the empire combining all earlier empires was Rome.

p: Not the "living creatures" of chapter 4. A wild, hunting animal.
b: Thērion is a wild or dangerous animal, used for animals in the arena where Christians were killed. The word appears 39 times in Revelation: 38 times for the beasts of chapters 11–20, and once for the wild animals of 6:8. The heavenly creatures of chapter 4 are zōa, "living ones."

p: Rumors said Nero had not died, or would return from the dead.
b: Nero killed himself in AD 68 with a sword wound to the throat. Rumors spread that he was alive in the East and would return; at least three impostors appeared (Tacitus, Histories 2.8; Suetonius, Nero 57). Others link the healed head to Rome surviving the chaos of AD 69. Futurists expect a future ruler who survives or fakes a fatal wound.

t: A counterfeit of "Who is like God?"
p: The people’s cry parodies Israel’s song, and the name Michael.
b: "Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?" was Israel's song after the Red Sea (Exodus 15:11). The name Michael means "Who is like God?" Many scholars note the parody of Exodus 15. My addition: placed just after Michael's victory in chapter 12, the crowd's question "Who is like the beast?" answers Michael's own name with the wrong answer.

p: "Was given," "was allowed": the beast’s power is on loan, for a set time.
b: The verb "was given" appears again and again in chapter 13 (verses 5, 7, 14, 15). The beast's authority comes from the dragon (13:2), but the time limit comes from God. Forty-two months is three and a half years, Daniel's "a time, times, and half a time" for the little horn's rule (Daniel 7:25; Daniel 12:7), and the length of the drought in Elijah's day as Jesus and James tell it (Luke 4:25; James 5:17), which lies behind the two witnesses of 11:6. Some also see an echo of Israel's 42 camps in the wilderness (Numbers 33).

p: Daniel 7:21: the horn made war with the holy ones and overpowered them.
b: The words come from Daniel 7:21, where the little horn on the fourth beast "made war with the holy ones" and prevailed against them, until the Ancient of Days came and the holy ones received the kingdom (Daniel 7:22). With 13:1–2, it marks the sea beast as Daniel's fourth beast and its little horn. Daniel's vision also gives the ending: the time is set, and the kingdom goes to the holy ones. Some old manuscripts lack this sentence; see the variant.

t: What happened "since the world was made"?
p: Names written since creation, or the Lamb slain since creation?
b: In the Greek, the phrase comes right after "the Lamb who was slaughtered," so word order favors "the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world" (KJV, NIV): the cross planned before creation (compare 1 Peter 1:19–20). But 17:8 uses the same phrase with names "written in the book of life since the world was made," and no Lamb, which favors "names written from the foundation of the world" (ESV, NRSV). The Plain follows 17:8 against the word order. The verse is also cited in the debate over election (compare 3:5; Ephesians 1:4).

a: another beast coming up out of the earth
p: Later called "the false prophet." It looks like a lamb, but speaks like a dragon.
b: Readers have seen: the priests of the imperial cult in Asia (preterists, many scholars); the papacy (Reformers); a future religious leader (futurists); or any religion that serves state power (idealists). From the 1850s, Seventh-day Adventist writers identified it with the United States, a "lamb-like" young nation with two horns (civil and religious liberty).

p: A saying from Jeremiah 15:2 and 43:11, turned from judgment into a call to endure.
b: Jeremiah 15:2 lists the fates God has assigned to faithless Judah: those meant for death, to death; those meant for the sword, to the sword; those meant for captivity, to captivity (compare Jeremiah 43:11). John borrows the pattern, but here the people facing captivity and the sword are the saints. The point is not that they deserve it, but that the beast's power is limited and allowed (13:5, 7), and that endurance, not fighting back, is their part. The manuscripts differ in both halves of the saying; see the variants.

p: The same verb Revelation uses for Jesus rising from the dead.
b: The Greek says only that the beast "lived," in the past tense: it had the sword wound "and lived." Revelation uses the same verb for Jesus, the one who died and came back to life (2:8), and for the martyrs who come to life in 20:4. The head of the beast also looked slaughtered (13:3), the word used of the Lamb in 5:6. The beast is a counterfeit Lamb, with its own death and return to life; 17:8 adds that it once was, now is not, and will come again. English Bibles that say "and yet lived" hide the parody.

a: give breath to the beast's image
p: Ancient temples had statues that seemed to speak, and priests who staged wonders.
b: Ancient writers describe hollow statues that "spoke" and tricks that made fire appear. Lucian (2nd century) mocked the false prophet Alexander, who made a snake-god appear to speak. In Asia, cities competed to build imperial temples with large emperor statues.

a: a mark on their right hand or on their forehead
p: The Greek says "on," not "in." Charagma was a stamp or seal.
b: KJV: "to receive a mark in their right hand, or in their foreheads." The Greek epi means "on." The English "in" has fed ideas about implanted chips. Charagma was the word for a stamp: the emperor's image on a coin, or an official seal on a sales contract. The mark copies God's seal on the forehead (7:3; 14:1) and the command to bind God's word on the hand and forehead (Deuteronomy 6:8).
orig: χάραγμα ἐπὶ τῆς χειρὸς (charagma epi tēs cheiros)

p: Guild membership and markets were tied to the worship of patron gods and the emperor.
b: In cities like Thyatira, trade guilds held feasts honoring patron gods, and markets displayed the emperor's image. Roman coins bore his image and titles. Refusing to take part could cost a Christian their livelihood, a kind of pressure the letters of chapters 2–3 already describe.

p: A name spelled in numbers? A number of imperfection? Readers have counted for 1,900 years.
b: Translation: arithmos anthrōpou can be "the number of a man" (a particular person) or "a human number" (a number people can work out), as the angel's measure in 21:17 is a human measure. Gematria: Greek and Hebrew letters were also numbers, so a name had a number. "Nero Caesar" spelled in Hebrew letters, נרון קסר, adds up to 666, a spelling found in a document from Wadi Murabba'at; the Latin-style spelling without the final n gives 616, the number in some manuscripts (see the variant). Irenaeus (about AD 180) tried names such as Euanthas, Lateinos and Teitan, preferred Teitan, and warned against being sure (Against Heresies 5.30.3). Idealists: six falls short of seven, three times over. Historicists have counted papal titles, futurists expect a future ruler. The views are set out further on the 13:16–18 card.

p: Psalm 2: "I myself have put my king in place on my holy mountain, on Zion."
b: Psalm 2:6 sets God's anointed king on Zion against the rebellious nations, which is exactly the contrast with chapter 13. Joel 2:32 promises that on Mount Zion there will be survivors who escape. Hebrews 12:22 speaks of "the heavenly Jerusalem," Mount Zion, as something believers have already come to.

p: Chapter 13 marks people with the beast’s name. Chapter 14 shows God’s.
b: The two chapters are set side by side: the beast's mark and name (13:16–17) versus the Lamb's and Father's names (14:1). The high priest wore "Holy to the LORD" on his forehead (Exodus 28:36–38). Everyone belongs to someone.

a: did not soil themselves with women
p: A soldier’s purity before holy war? Faithfulness without idolatry?
b: The 144,000 "did not soil themselves with women, for they are virgins." Parthenos is usually used of women but here describes men. Many scholars read it as the purity rule for soldiers in holy war (Deuteronomy 23:9–10; 1 Samuel 21:5), which fits the army-style census of chapter 7. Others read faithfulness with no idolatry, which the prophets call adultery. A few read literal celibacy.

p: The first part of the harvest, given to God, promising more to come.
b: Firstfruits were the first sheaves offered at the feast before the full harvest (Leviticus 23:10). James 1:18 calls believers firstfruits, so to speak, of the things God made. In this chapter, a full harvest follows (14:14–16).

p: A last call to repent. Seventh-day Adventists see their mission here.
b: The first angel calls every nation to "fear God and give him glory" and worship the Creator. Adventist tradition reads 14:6–12 as God's last message, centered on the Sabbath (Exodus 20:11). Most others read a final offer of grace to all nations before the harvest.

a: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the Great
p: "Fallen! Fallen is Babylon!" (Isaiah 21:9).
b: The cry is from Isaiah 21:9, and "Babylon the great" from Daniel 4:30, where Nebuchadnezzar boasts of the city he built. The wine comes from Jeremiah: "A cup of gold, that was Babylon, in the hand of the LORD, getting the whole earth drunk" (Jeremiah 51:7). The Greek word for her "raging" passion, thymos, is also the word for God's anger in 14:10: the wine she pours becomes the wine she must drink.

a: mixed undiluted in the cup of his wrath
p: Strong wine, not cut with water: the prophets' cup of judgment.
b: Ancient wine was normally mixed with water before drinking. Akratos means "unmixed," full strength, so the phrase is a deliberate paradox: "mixed undiluted." The image is the prophets' cup of judgment: "the LORD holds a cup in his hand, its wine foaming, full of spiced mix" (Psalm 75:8); Jerusalem had drunk "the cup of his fury" (Isaiah 51:17); and Jeremiah was told to make the nations drink the cup of the wine of God's wrath (Jeremiah 25:15–29). "Fire and sulfur" recalls the judgment on Sodom, where "the LORD rained sulfur and fire" (Genesis 19:24), and on Edom (Isaiah 34:9).

a: The smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever
p: Eternal conscious punishment, final destruction, or symbol?
