b: Traditional readers see eternal conscious punishment. Others (conditional immortality, or "annihilationism") note that the image is copied from Isaiah 34:10, where of Edom "its smoke will keep going up forever" (Isaiah 34:10), yet the land is then inhabited by wild animals, so the image means complete, permanent destruction. A third group stresses that the scene is a warning meant to lead to repentance (14:7, 12). The churches' own answers, which really do conflict, are set side by side in the "Where Christians differ" card at chapter 20 (20:10, 14–15).

p: Faith in Jesus, faithfulness to Jesus, or Jesus' own faithfulness?
b: The Greek is as open as the English: "they keep ... the faith of Jesus." It may mean their faith in Jesus (NIV, ESV), their faithfulness to him, or the faith Jesus himself kept and taught, which they hold on to (KJV keeps "the faith of Jesus"). "Keep" suits something received and guarded, like the commandments in the same line. It is the same question as "the testimony of Jesus" at 12:17 (see the note there). Seventh-day Adventists read 14:12 with 12:17 as the mark of the last-days remnant, keeping all God's commandments, the Sabbath included.

a: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord
p: The second blessing of the book, for martyrs and all believers.
b: "Rest" answers 14:11, where the beast's worshipers have "no rest." The verse echoes Hebrews 4:9–10 on entering God's rest. It is often read at Christian funerals.

a: someone like a son of man
p: Christ, gathering his people? Or an angel of judgment?
b: The "son of man" on a cloud with a gold crown seems to be Christ (1:13; Daniel 7:13). The grain harvest may picture the gathering of believers (Matthew 13:30; Mark 4:29); the grape harvest that follows is judgment. Some read both harvests as judgment. Notice that an angel tells him when to reap, as Jesus said only the Father knows the hour (Mark 13:32).

p: The Greek gives 1,600 stadia. Like most numbers here, it carries meaning.
b: A stadion was about 607 feet, so 1,600 stadia is about 184 miles. The number is 40 × 40 or 4 × 4 × 100, both suggesting the whole world. Some point out it is close to the length of Israel from Tyre to the border of Egypt. Converting it to miles hides the pattern, so the Plain keeps "stadia," as most literal translations do.

a: a sea of glass mixed with fire
p: Israel sang beside the sea after Pharaoh’s army drowned.
b: Exodus 15: having crossed the sea, Moses and Israel sing. Here the conquerors of the beast stand beside a sea of glass and sing "the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb." The fire may suggest judgment or the pillar of fire.

a: the song of Moses, the slave of God, and the song of the Lamb
t: A song of Moses that never mentions their own victory
p: Exodus 15 celebrates Israel’s rescue. This song celebrates God and the nations.
b: Exodus 15 sings of Israel's escape and the enemy drowned. Remarkably, the song in Revelation 15:3–4 never mentions the singers' victory at all. It draws on Psalm 86:9 and Jeremiah 10:7 and says that all the nations will come and worship. Richard Bauckham pointed this out (The Climax of Prophecy). "Slave of God" was Moses' title of honor (Joshua 14:7; Deuteronomy 34:5, Hebrew ebed YHWH). My addition: since the beast's followers just heard a call to repent (14:6–7), the song of the saved is about the nations turning to God, not about their own triumph.

p: The tabernacle in the wilderness, where the covenant tablets were kept.
b: The "tent of the testimony" (Numbers 9:15; 17:7) held the ark and the tablets of the law. Judgment comes from the place of God's covenant. The smoke filling the temple recalls Exodus 40:34–35 and Isaiah 6:4.

p: Sores, blood, darkness: the plagues of Egypt again, now complete.
b: The bowls follow the order of the trumpets: land, sea, rivers, sun, darkness, Euphrates, storm. The trumpets struck a third; the bowls strike all. Sores were Egypt's sixth plague (Exodus 9:8–11), and they fall on those who carry the beast's mark.

t: Who is, who was, and no "who is coming"
p: God's threefold name loses its third part, because now he has come.
b: In 1:4 and 1:8 God is the one who is, who was, and who is coming. Here, as at 11:17, the angel says only "who is and who was." Most commentators (Bauckham, Koester) take the change as deliberate: the one who was to come has now come in judgment, so the future part is no longer future. The KJV's "and shalt be" comes from a guess by the editor Theodore Beza, not from any Greek manuscript; see the variant.
orig: ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν (ho ōn kai ho ēn)

a: you have given them blood to drink
p: They poured out blood; they receive blood.
b: The angel calls this just because the punishment matches the crime. The pattern of "measure for measure" runs through the book: Babylon receives the cup she mixed (18:6), and the destroyers of the earth are destroyed (11:18).

a: They did not repent and give him glory
p: Twice the bowls say people did not repent. Repentance was still possible.
b: Twice the bowls note that people did not repent (16:9, 11), just as in 9:20–21, and three times that they insulted God (16:9, 11, 21). If the plagues were only punishment, there would be no reason to note that people refused to repent. My reading: even the last judgments in Revelation are designed as a final appeal, like the plagues of Egypt, which were meant so that "Egypt will know that I am the LORD" (Exodus 7:5).

a: the kings from where the sun rises
p: For John’s readers, the Parthians. For later readers, many candidates.
b: Rome's eastern rivals the Parthians crossed the Euphrates more than once, and the Nero legend said Nero would return with them. In history and in the 20th century, readers have suggested Muslims, Japan, China, or other eastern powers. Cyrus took Babylon by diverting the Euphrates (Herodotus 1.191), and Isaiah 44:27–28 links the drying of rivers to Cyrus.

p: Egypt’s second plague, and a symbol of unclean things.
b: Frogs swarmed Egypt (Exodus 8:2–7), and Egypt's magicians copied the sign. The spirits are "unclean" (akatharta, the Gospels' word for the spirits Jesus drove out), and frogs were unclean animals (Leviticus 11:10). Some Persian texts call frogs creatures of the evil spirit Ahriman. Three spirits come from the three mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet.

a: Look, I am coming like a thief!
p: Right before the kings gather, Jesus speaks directly to the reader.
b: Verse 15 breaks the scene with a beatitude about staying awake and keeping your clothes on, which echoes the warnings to Sardis (3:3–4) and Laodicea (3:18). My reading: John puts the call where you would least expect it, at the battle, because the real fight at Armageddon is about the reader staying faithful, not about military strategy.

p: Har Megiddo, "mountain of Megiddo." But Megiddo is a hill on a plain.
b: It is not a word that means "the end of the world." NASB prints it "Har-Magedon." Oddly, Megiddo is a mound on a plain, not a mountain. Suggestions include nearby Mount Carmel, where Elijah faced the prophets of Baal, or a play on Hebrew har mo'ed, "mount of assembly," where the king of Babylon tried to set up his throne (Isaiah 14:13). Who gathers the kings there? The Greek verb is singular. With a neuter plural subject that is normal Greek, so the spirits of 16:13–14 are the likely subject, but some read God as the one who gathers them (compare 17:17; 20:8), and the Plain leaves it open as the Greek does.
orig: Ἁρμαγεδών (Harmagedōn), from Hebrew har Megiddo, "mountain of Megiddo"

p: One word in Greek, spoken from the throne, as Jesus spoke one word from the cross.
b: The voice from the throne says a single Greek word, gegonen, "it has happened, it is done." It is said again over the new creation in 21:6. Many readers hear an echo of Jesus' last word on the cross in John's Gospel, "It is finished" (John 19:30), though the Greek word there is a different one (tetelestai). What began at the cross is carried through to the end.

p: Jerusalem, or Babylon/Rome? The verse names Babylon next.
b: Revelation calls Babylon "the great city" again and again (17:18; 18:10, 16, 18, 19, 21), and the verse goes straight on to Babylon, so most readers take the city split in three to be Babylon, that is, Rome or the world's power center. But 11:8 called Jerusalem "the great city" too, the city where their Lord was crucified, and many preterists read 16:19 as Jerusalem, divided into factions during the Roman siege of AD 70, with Babylon's judgment following. Futurists often see a literal earthquake splitting a future Jerusalem (compare Zechariah 14:4).

p: The Greek says the weight of a talent, very roughly 60 to 90 pounds.
b: A talent was the largest weight in common use; it varied by region and period, and common estimates run from about 60 to 90 pounds. Josephus says that during the Roman siege of Jerusalem the catapults threw white stones weighing a talent, and that watchmen shouted a warning when one was coming (Jewish War 5.269–273). The Greek manuscripts have them shout "The son is coming"; many editors correct it to "The stone is coming," explaining it as a play on Hebrew ben, "son," and eben, "stone." Some preterists make much of the manuscript reading. Preterists see the siege as the fulfillment; others read a supernatural storm, as in Exodus 9:24 and Joshua 10:11.

a: the great prostitute who sits on many waters
p: Jeremiah said this to ancient Babylon, which sat on the Euphrates.
b: Jeremiah 51:13: "You who dwell beside many waters, great in treasures, your end has come." Babylon sat on the Euphrates and its canals. 17:15 explains the waters as nations. The prophets often called idolatrous cities prostitutes (Isaiah 23:16–17 of Tyre; Nahum 3:4 of Nineveh; Ezekiel 16 of Jerusalem).

p: Is "Mystery" part of her name? The Greek allows "a name, a mystery."
b: KJV prints "MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT" all in capitals, as if "Mystery" is part of the name. The Greek can mean "a name written, a mystery," meaning a symbolic name (compare "symbolically called" in 11:8). ESV: "a name of mystery." It warns you not to look for a city that is literally named Babylon.

a: drunk with the blood of the saints
p: Nero’s persecution in AD 64 killed many Christians in Rome.
b: Tacitus (Annals 15.44) describes Christians in Rome being torn by dogs, crucified, and burned as torches in Nero's gardens. Peter and Paul were remembered as martyrs there. Preterists who read Babylon as Jerusalem point instead to Matthew 23:35–37.

p: Every ancient reader knew which city sat on seven hills.
b: Rome was "the city of seven hills" (Latin poets: Virgil, Horace, Ovid, Martial). A coin of Vespasian shows the goddess Roma reclining on seven hills. The angel adds that the heads are also seven kings, so the image is doing double duty.

p: Which emperors? The count changes the date of the book.
b: Starting from Augustus: Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, Nero (five fallen), Galba or Vespasian (one is), and so on, depending on whether the three short reigns of AD 69 count. Starting from Julius Caesar shifts the list. Some say the seven are not emperors at all but seven empires (Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece, Rome, and one to come), the common futurist view. Others read seven as a symbol of the full line of rulers. (The KJV starts this verse with "And there are seven kings." This site follows the verse division of the Greek editions, which end 17:9 with those words.)

t: An eighth who belongs to the seven
p: Eight is the number of resurrection in early Christian thought.
b: Early Christians called Sunday "the eighth day," the day of the resurrection (Barnabas 15:9). The Greek says only "he himself is an eighth"; "king" is understood from 17:10. The beast "was, and is not, and will be here" (17:8), a parody of God's name in 1:4, the one who is, who was, and who is coming. My speculation: the "eighth" is a counterfeit resurrection, a revived old power posing as a new beginning. Interestingly, the Greek letters of "Jesus" (Iēsous) add up to 888, which some ancient Christians noticed (Sibylline Oracles 1.324–30), compared with the beast's 666.

a: Lord of lords and King of kings
p: Deuteronomy 10:17 and Daniel 4:37 in the Greek.
b: Deuteronomy 10:17: "the LORD your God is the God of gods and the Lord of lords." In the Greek version of Daniel 4:37, Nebuchadnezzar calls God "Lord of lords and King of kings." The title appears again on the rider in 19:16, in reverse order.

p: The beast turns on the city that rode it.
b: The beast and its allies destroy the prostitute. Evil in Revelation is self-destructive, and God "gave it to their hearts" (17:17). Preterists see Rome destroying Jerusalem; others, Rome burning in AD 64 or AD 69 (when the Capitol was burned in civil war); futurists a future betrayal. My reading: the scene shows that the economic system (the prostitute) and the political power (the beast) are allies of convenience, and the second will devour the first.

p: Isaiah and Jeremiah pictured fallen Babylon as a haunt of wild creatures.
b: Isaiah 13:21–22; 34:11–14 and Jeremiah 50:39 describe Babylon and Edom becoming deserts haunted by owls, jackals and goat-demons. Ancient Babylon did become ruins, mostly abandoned by the 2nd century AD.

a: Come out of her, my people
p: Jeremiah 51:45: "Come out of her, my people! Let each one save his life."
b: Jeremiah 51:45 and Isaiah 48:20; 52:11 call the exiles out of Babylon. Paul uses similar words for separation from idolatry (2 Corinthians 6:17). The reason here is to avoid sharing her sins, which suggests a spiritual and economic leaving, not only a physical one.

t: "I will never sit as a widow"
p: The boast of ancient Babylon in Isaiah 47.
b: Isaiah 47:7–9: "You said, 'I will be the lady forever, for all time'... I will never sit as a widow... In an instant, on one day, the two will both come to you." Revelation copies the boast and the "one day" (18:8).

p: Chapter 18 is modeled on Ezekiel’s funeral song for Tyre.
b: Ezekiel 26–28 laments the trading city of Tyre: kings, merchants and sailors mourn, throw dust on their heads, and ask, "Who is like Tyre?" (Ezekiel 27:32). Ezekiel 27:12–24 lists Tyre's cargo, like 18:12–13 here.

p: Slave traders called slaves "bodies." John adds: they are human souls.
b: In Greek commerce, sōmata ("bodies") was the standard word for slaves. The list runs in one grammatical form up to "bodies," then John breaks the pattern and adds "and human souls," echoing Ezekiel 27:13, where Tyre's traders deal in nefesh adam, literally "human souls." Some translations join the two ("slaves, that is, human lives"); the Greek simply adds the second phrase with "and." The cargo list ends with the item that exposes the rest. Rome's economy ran on slavery, perhaps 10 to 20 percent of the population.
orig: σωμάτων, καὶ ψυχὰς ἀνθρώπων (sōmatōn, kai psychas anthrōpōn)

a: a stone like a huge millstone
t: A stone thrown into the river
p: Jeremiah had a scroll tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates.
b: Jeremiah 51:63–64: "tie a stone on it and throw it into the middle of the Euphrates... Like this Babylon will sink and will not come up." Jesus spoke of a millstone hung from the neck of anyone who trips up one of the little ones (Matthew 18:6).

a: The voice of bridegroom and bride
t: The bride moves to another city
p: The wedding voices leave Babylon and are heard again at the Lamb’s wedding.
b: Jeremiah used this line for Jerusalem's ruin (Jeremiah 7:34; 25:10). In the very next chapter, the wedding of the Lamb is announced (19:7). My observation: the book takes the bride and the wedding music away from Babylon, and moves them to the new city, which is itself "made ready like a bride" (21:2). It is a tale of two cities, and of two women.

p: Its only uses in the New Testament are here, four times.
b: Hallelu-yah means "Praise the LORD." It occurs four times in 19:1–6 and nowhere else in the New Testament. Psalms 113–118 (the Hallel) were sung at Passover, and Psalm 104:35 ends with the first hallelujah of the psalter, right after a prayer that sinners vanish from the earth.

p: The prophets called Israel God’s bride. Jesus called himself the bridegroom.
b: Isaiah 54:5: "For your husband is your Maker." In Hosea 2:19–20 God says to his people, "I will pledge you to myself in marriage forever." Jesus called himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19–20) and told wedding banquet parables (Matthew 22:1–14; 25:1–13). Paul applies it to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:25–32).

a: the right deeds of the saints
p: "Righteousness of saints" is plural: righteous acts.
b: KJV: "the fine linen is the righteousness of saints." The Greek is plural: "the righteous acts of the saints" (NKJV, ESV, NIV). The verse also says the linen was "given" to the bride to wear (edothē). So it holds both together: a gift, and a life lived out.
orig: τὰ δικαιώματα τῶν ἁγίων (ta dikaiōmata tōn hagiōn)

t: Even John got it wrong, twice
p: The book’s visionary bows to an angel, twice. A warning about being dazzled.
b: John falls before the angel here and again in 22:8–9. The one who saw the vision was overwhelmed by its messenger. Several scholars suggest it warns against angel worship (compare Colossians 2:18). My application: if John himself could misplace his awe, readers should be humble about their interpretations, and keep worship on God alone, not on the prophecy or its interpreters.

a: the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy
p: Jesus's own witness, or witness about Jesus? The Greek allows both.
b: The Greek "testimony of Jesus" can mean the testimony Jesus himself gave (he is "the faithful witness," 1:5), or the testimony his followers give about him. Many English Bibles pick one ("the testimony about Jesus"). This translation keeps "of Jesus," as the Greek has it, here and in 12:17 and 20:4. Richard Bauckham and Craig Koester read it mainly as Jesus's own witness, which the Spirit carries on through Christian prophets: what Jesus testified is what moves every true prophet. Others read it as witness about Jesus, so that all true prophecy points to him. Many readers think John means both, since the church's witness repeats his. Either way the angel's point holds: he and John stand on the same footing, fellow slaves who hold that witness, so worship belongs to God alone.

p: Christ’s white horse answers the conqueror of 6:2.
b: In a Roman triumph the victorious general rode through the city in a chariot drawn by four horses, white ones on the grandest occasions; white horses meant victory. The rider's eyes and sword repeat 1:14–16. He judges "in righteousness," as the king does in Isaiah 11:4.

p: The robe is bloodied before the battle starts. Three readings, and mine.
b: Isaiah 63:1–3 pictures the LORD coming from Edom in red clothes, stained from treading the winepress: "Their juice spattered on my clothes" (Isaiah 63:3). Readers take the blood three ways. The enemies' blood, as in Isaiah 63: the rider comes as judge (David Aune and Grant Osborne, among others). The martyrs' blood: some link the robe to the winepress of 14:20 and see the blood of Christ's faithful witnesses, whom he now vindicates. His own blood: the robe is already dipped before any fighting is described, the armies behind him are in clean white, and elsewhere in the book the blood linked with Christ is always his own (Richard Bauckham and others). I lean to the third: the Word of God conquers as the Lamb who was slaughtered (5:6), and the only weapon used is the sword of his mouth (19:15, 21). Some manuscripts read "sprinkled" for "dipped"; see the variant.

a: he will shepherd them with an iron rod
p: Psalm 2:9, the third time Revelation uses it (2:27; 12:5).
b: The Hebrew of Psalm 2:9 reads "You will crush them with an iron rod" (Psalm 2:9). The Greek translation of the Psalm read the same Hebrew letters as "you will shepherd them," and Revelation follows that Greek here, as in 2:27 and 12:5. A shepherd's rod guards the flock and breaks the wolves. The Psalm's king is now the rider, and his only weapon is the sword from his mouth (Isaiah 11:4).

p: Ezekiel 39: a feast for birds over Gog’s armies.
b: In Ezekiel 39:17–20 God tells the prophet to call every kind of bird and wild animal to gather from all around to the sacrifice he is slaughtering for them, a feast on the flesh of warriors and princes. Revelation sets this "supper of God" against the "wedding supper of the Lamb" (19:9). Every reader is invited to one of the two meals.

t: Gehenna and the lake of fire
p: Jesus spoke of Gehenna, a valley outside Jerusalem.
b: The "lake of fire" is unique to Revelation. It draws on the fire of Sodom (Genesis 19:24), Isaiah 66:24, Daniel 7:11 (the beast handed over to be burned with fire), and Jesus's Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom where children had been sacrificed (Jeremiah 7:31). 1 Enoch 90:24–26 has fallen angels thrown into a fiery abyss.

p: A literal future reign, the church age, or a golden age before Christ returns?
b: Premillennial: Christ returns first and reigns 1,000 years on earth. Amillennial: the thousand years is the present church age, with Satan bound by Christ's victory (Matthew 12:29). Postmillennial: the gospel will spread and bring a long golden age before Christ returns. The early church had both premillennial (Irenaeus) and non-literal (Origen, later Augustine) readers.

p: Jesus said he had come to tie up the strong man.
b: Jesus: "how could anyone break into a strong man's house and seize his goods, without first tying the strong man up?" (Matthew 12:29). Amillennialists read 20:2 as that binding, with Satan unable to "lead the nations astray" (stop the gospel) during the church age. Premillennialists note that Satan is very active in the New Testament (1 Peter 5:8), so the binding must be future. Compare Isaiah 24:21–22, where the powers on high are locked in a dungeon "and after many days they will be called to account."

t: Who sits on the thrones, and who reigns?
p: Two small Greek phrases leave the scene more open than most English Bibles do.
b: 1. "Judgment was given to them." This can mean they were given authority to judge (as in 1 Corinthians 6:2 and Matthew 19:28), or that a verdict was given in their favor, as in Daniel 7:22, where judgment is given for the holy ones of the Most High and they receive the kingdom. The two can go together: vindicated, then sharing the rule. Who sits on the thrones is not said: the martyrs, the apostles, the twenty-four elders of 4:4, or all the faithful. 2. "And those who had not worshiped the beast." The Greek joins this with "and" (kai hoitines). Many read one group, the beheaded, described further; this site's Plain keeps the "and," which also allows a second, wider group: everyone who refused the beast, whether killed or not. David Aune and G. K. Beale both discuss the two readings. On what "came to life" means, see the note at 20:5.
orig: κρίμα ἐδόθη αὐτοῖς ... καὶ οἵτινες οὐ προσεκύνησαν (krima edothē autois ... kai hoitines ou prosekynēsan)

p: The Greek word means "beheaded with an axe," an old Roman penalty.
b: The Greek pepelekismenōn comes from pelekys, "axe." The axe was the old penalty of the Roman Republic; by the first century, Roman citizens condemned to death were usually beheaded with the sword. Tradition says Paul, a citizen, was beheaded in Rome. John may use the old word simply for execution by Roman authority.

p: A bodily resurrection, or new life in Christ?
b: Premillennialists: a bodily resurrection of believers before the millennium, with the rest raised after. Amillennialists: either the new birth (John 5:24–29, where Jesus speaks of a spiritual resurrection now and a bodily one later), or the souls of martyrs entering heaven. The verb "came to life" (ezēsan) is the one used of Jesus's resurrection in 2:8, which supports a real coming back to life, and the same verb in 20:5 is used of the rest of the dead. Many amillennial readers (following Augustine) translate it "they lived," meaning the martyrs live and reign with Christ in heaven now. Note also that some manuscripts lack the first sentence of 20:5; see the variant.

t: Gog of the land of Magog
p: Ezekiel 38–39: an invasion from the far north after Israel is restored.
b: In Ezekiel, Gog is the ruler of the land of Magog who invades restored Israel and is destroyed by fire from heaven (Ezekiel 38:22; 39:6). In later Jewish tradition, Gog and Magog became two peoples representing all the nations. Readers have identified them with Scythians, Goths, Huns, Mongols, Turks and Russia.

a: where the beast and the false prophet are too
p: The Greek has no verb here. English has to supply one, and the choice matters.
b: Literally: "where also the beast and the false prophet." The KJV supplies "are," as this translation does: the two thrown in at 19:20 are still there a thousand years later. Some versions supply "had been thrown," which describes only their past arrival. The next words, "they will be tormented day and night forever and ever," are the strongest text for unending punishment, and readers who hold that view stress "are." Readers who hold conditional immortality reply that the beast and the false prophet are symbols of empire and false religion, not individual persons, and that "forever and ever" can describe a result that never ends. See "Where Christians differ" on this chapter page.
orig: ὅπου καὶ τὸ θηρίον καὶ ὁ ψευδοπροφήτης (hopou kai to thērion kai ho pseudoprophētēs)

p: From Daniel 7:10: "The court sat, and books were opened."
b: Daniel 7:10 and 12:1–2 picture books at the final judgment. Judgment is "according to their deeds," and yet entry depends on the book of life (20:15), the Lamb's book (21:27). Works show who people are; the Lamb's book shows whose they are.

a: Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire
p: The first thing to be destroyed at the end is death.
b: Death and Hades ride as the fourth horseman (6:8). Here they are thrown into the lake of fire. Paul: "The last enemy to be done away with is death" (1 Corinthians 15:26). My reading: the lake of fire is presented as the destruction of the powers that ruin creation, which is why it is called "the second death." Whatever one concludes about its human victims, the text's first emphasis is that death itself dies.

a: a new heaven and a new earth
p: "For look, I am creating new heavens and a new earth" (Isaiah 65:17).
b: Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; 2 Peter 3:13. The Greek word for new, kainos, often means new in quality, renewed, rather than brand new. Debate: is this creation destroyed and replaced, or renewed (Romans 8:19–22)?

a: the sea is no longer there
p: Sea meant chaos, the beast’s home, and the gulf between John and his churches.
b: The sea is where the beast rose (13:1), where Babylon's trade sailed (18:17), and where the dead lay (20:13). For John on Patmos, it also separated him from his churches. No more sea means nothing left that threatens or divides.

a: God's tent is with human beings
p: Skēnē, "tent," echoes the Hebrew Shekinah, God’s dwelling presence.
b: Skēnē means tent or tabernacle. It sounds like the Hebrew shekinah, God's dwelling glory, and its verb is used in John 1:14: "the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us" (eskēnōsen). Leviticus 26:11–12 and Ezekiel 37:27 promise that God will dwell with his people: "I will be your God, and you will be my people" (Leviticus 26:12). On the plural "peoples" here, see the variant.
orig: ἡ σκηνὴ τοῦ θεοῦ (hē skēnē tou theou), "the tent of God"

a: He will wipe every tear out of their eyes
p: Isaiah 25:8: "He will swallow death up for all time."
b: Isaiah 25:8: "The Lord GOD will wipe the tears off every face." Isaiah 65:19: "The sound of weeping and the sound of crying out will no longer be heard there." This promise was given to the multitude in 7:17, and now it is fulfilled for everyone in the city.

a: I am making all things new
p: Isaiah heard God promise a new thing; here it is done.
b: Isaiah 43:19: "Look at me, about to do something new." In Isaiah the new thing is a road home from exile through the desert; here it is the whole creation. Paul uses the same idea for a person in Christ: "a new creation" (2 Corinthians 5:17). This is the first time since 1:8 that the book plainly has God himself speak.

p: Isaiah 55:1 invites the thirsty to come and drink for free.
b: Isaiah 55:1: "Hey! All you who are thirsty, come to the water! And you who have no money, come, buy grain and eat!" Jesus made the same call (John 7:37). The gift is free (dōrean, "as a gift"), the same word as in 22:17.

p: The promise to David's heir, now given to everyone who wins the victory.
b: The Greek is singular: "I will be his God, and he will be my son." It echoes God's promise about David's heir, "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me" (2 Samuel 7:14), and the king's adoption in Psalm 2:7: "You are my son." What was promised to the king is now promised to each person who wins the victory, as in the seven letters (2:26–27; 3:21). "Son" here is the heir's title, and it includes daughters: Paul quotes the same promise as "you will be my sons and daughters" (2 Corinthians 6:18). Compare Romans 8:14–17, where all God's children are heirs.
orig: αὐτὸς ἔσται μοι υἱός (autos estai moi huios)

a: the names of the twelve tribes of the Israelites
t: Israel and the apostles in one city
p: The gates bear Israel’s tribes, the foundations the apostles.
b: The city is built on both: twelve tribes on the gates (from Ezekiel 48:30–35) and twelve apostles on the foundations. Many read this as the one people of God from both covenants. Some dispensationalists see Israel and the church as distinct groups who share the same city.

t: The size of the known world
p: 12,000 stadia is a symbolic number, and also a huge one.
b: 12,000 stadia (about 1,400 miles) is a symbolic number (12 × 1,000), the number of God's people multiplied. My own rough estimate: a square 1,400 miles on each side would cover most of the eastern Mediterranean world, from Greece to Mesopotamia. My speculation: John's readers may have pictured the new Jerusalem as large enough to cover all their known world, so the holy of holies becomes as large as the empire it replaces.

t: Jewels of the high priest and of Zion
p: The high priest’s breastplate, and Isaiah’s jeweled city.
b: Exodus 28:17–21 has twelve stones engraved with the names of the tribes. Isaiah 54:11–12: "lay your foundations with lapis lazuli... your gates of sparkling stones." Tobit 13:16–17 (Scripture in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament) also imagines Jerusalem rebuilt with sapphire, emerald and precious stone. Some of the Greek stone names are uncertain, so English Bibles differ (the third stone, chalkēdōn, is "chalcedony" here; some versions say "agate").

t: Pearl gates and the pearl of great price
p: Jesus told of a merchant who sold everything for one pearl.
b: Pearls were the most valuable gems in the Roman world. In Matthew 13:45–46 the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant who sold everything to buy one priceless pearl. My suggestion: John may want readers to recall that parable, especially after the merchants' lament over Babylon's pearls (18:12, 16). Babylon's merchants lose their pearls; the city of God is entered through them. (The "pearly gates" with Saint Peter as gatekeeper is later folklore.)

a: I did not see a temple in it
p: The whole city is the Most Holy Place.
b: The city is as tall as it is long and wide (21:16). Most readers picture a cube, like the Most Holy Place (1 Kings 6:20), though some picture a pyramid. Only the high priest entered it, once a year. Now everyone lives in God's presence, and "they will see his face" (22:4), which even Moses could not (Exodus 33:20).

a: the kings of the earth bring their glory into it
t: The kings of the earth come back
p: The same kings who served Babylon now bring their glory to the city.
b: "The kings of the earth" committed sin with Babylon (17:2; 18:9) and fought the Lamb (19:19). Now they bring their glory into the new Jerusalem, as in Isaiah 60:3–11. Many scholars (Bauckham, Caird) see a note of hope for the nations here. My own reading is cautious: the text gives no timeline, but its final picture of "the nations" is of healing (22:2), not destruction.

a: a river of the water of life
p: Ezekiel 47: a river flows from the temple and heals everything.
b: Ezekiel 47:1–12: water flows from under the temple, growing deeper, making salt water fresh, with fruit trees on both banks whose leaves heal. Zechariah 14:8 and Psalm 46:4 ("A river! Its channels gladden the city of God") join in. Genesis 2:10 has a river flowing out of Eden.

p: In a city with no more pain, the leaves are still "for healing the nations."
b: If there is no more pain (21:4), why healing? Some read it as a picture of fullness of life, others as a continuing process. My speculation: the leaves answer the curse of Babel and of the nations' long war against God. The nations arrive in the city with histories that need healing, and the tree from Eden provides it.

a: Nothing will be under a curse any longer
p: John quotes Zechariah 14:11, and the story goes back to Genesis 3.
b: The words come almost exactly from Zechariah 14:11, which in Hebrew says there will never again be a ḥerem, a ban of destruction, on Jerusalem, and that the city will live in safety. The Greek Old Testament there uses anathema; Revelation's katathema is its close cousin. Behind it stands the first curse: "the ground is cursed on your account" (Genesis 3:17). The Bible's story ends where it began, in a garden, with the curse removed.

p: Moses could not see God’s face and live. Here everyone does.
b: Exodus 33:20: "You cannot see my face, for no human being can see me and stay alive." Psalm 17:15: "I, in the right, will look upon your face." Jesus: "Blessed are those whose hearts are pure, because they will see God" (Matthew 5:8). The name on their foreheads recalls the high priest's gold plate (Exodus 28:36–38).

a: Do not seal up the words
p: Daniel was told to seal his book. John is told not to.
b: In Daniel 12:4 the angel tells Daniel to close up the words and seal the book until the time of the end. John is told the opposite, "because the time is near." Preterists stress that the nearness was for the first readers. Others see "the time of the end" as having begun with Christ (Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18).

a: Let the wrongdoer go on doing wrong
p: Daniel 12:10: at the end, the wicked keep on acting wickedly.
b: Daniel 12:10 says that at the end many will be purified and made white, but the wicked will go on acting wickedly, and none of them will understand. Revelation says the same with a warning edge: the time is near, so the choices people are making now will set. It is not a command to keep sinning but a statement that the hour for changing course is short.

p: Isaiah said the Lord GOD would come bringing his reward. Jesus says it of himself.
b: Isaiah 40:10: "Look, the Lord GOD comes in strength... Look, he brings his reward with him." Isaiah 62:11 repeats it for Daughter Zion. Jesus now speaks Isaiah's words about the Lord GOD as his own, and the next verse gives him God's own title, "the Alpha and the Omega."

p: A harsh word for people outside the covenant, used by Jews and by Paul.
b: Dogs in the ancient Near East were scavengers, not pets. The word was an insult for the unclean or for pagans, and Deuteronomy 23:18 may use it for male temple prostitutes. Paul uses it for false teachers (Philippians 3:2). The list matches 21:8.

p: Isaiah’s root of Jesse and Balaam’s star from Jacob, together.
b: "The Root of David" comes from Isaiah 11:1, 10 (see 5:5). "A star will march out of Jacob" is Balaam's prophecy (Numbers 24:17). The morning star was promised to Thyatira (2:28); now Jesus says he is that star.

a: The Spirit and the bride say, "Come!"
t: Who is being called to come?
p: "Come!" is said three times: to Jesus, to the hearer, to the thirsty.
b: The first "Come!" may be the church calling Jesus to return (22:20). The second invites each hearer to join that prayer. The third invites the thirsty to come and drink. My reading: the book ends by turning its four horsemen's "Come!" (6:1, 3, 5, 7), which summoned disasters, into a welcome. The same word that released judgment now opens the door to the water of life.

a: if anyone puts anything onto them
t: Do not add, do not take away
p: Moses gave the same warning for the law. It covers this book, not yet the whole Bible.
b: Deuteronomy 4:2: "Do not add anything to the word I am commanding you, and do not take anything away from it" (also Deuteronomy 12:32). The Greek keeps a play on words: whoever "puts on" more words, God will "put on" him the plagues. Many readers take the warning as sealing the whole Bible, but it speaks of "this book," the prophecy John wrote, at a time when the New Testament had not yet been gathered into one volume. See the chapter page.

p: The Greek form of the oldest Christian prayer, "Our Lord, come!"
b: Paul kept the Aramaic Maranatha in 1 Corinthians 16:22. The Didache (10:6) uses it in a communion prayer. The book that began "the time is near" ends with the church praying for the coming of the one it worships.

t: The word "antichrist" is not in Revelation
p: The word "antichrist" never appears in Revelation.
b: It appears only in 1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3 and 2 John 7, where John says "many antichrists" have already come. Revelation's figures are "the beast" and "the false prophet." Linking them to Paul's "man of lawlessness" (2 Thessalonians 2) and Daniel's "little horn" (Daniel 7:8) is a reasonable step, but it is an interpretation, not a quote.

a: They came to life and ruled with Christ for a thousand years
p: The whole doctrine of the millennium rests on this one passage.
b: The thousand years appear six times, all in Revelation 20, and nowhere else in the Bible as a reign. Every millennial view rests mostly on this one chapter, read alongside Old Testament promises such as Isaiah 11 and 65.

a: will never be harmed by the second death
t: The second death, first as a promise
p: Said first to martyrs: Rome can cause the first death, not the second.
b: The phrase "second death" was used in the Aramaic Targums for final exclusion from the world to come. Its first use in Revelation comforts a church facing prison and death (2:10). The first death is not the one to fear (Matthew 10:28). See chapter 21 for more.

t: The list starts with believers who give up
p: "Cowardly" and "faithless" come first, before murderers: a warning to the church.
b: Deiloi means cowards, those who shrink back under pressure; apistoi means faithless or unfaithful. In a book written to persecuted churches, these are people who deny Jesus to save themselves, the opposite of Antipas, who "did not deny" (2:13), and of the martyrs who "did not love their lives" (12:11). The verse is the dark twin of 21:7, "the one who wins the victory will inherit these things." Jesus: "whoever denies me in front of people, I too will deny that person in front of my Father in heaven" (Matthew 10:33).

p: An inheritance word. Everyone receives a share; the verse asks which one.
b: Meros means a portion or share, as in dividing an inheritance. Revelation uses it for those who have "a share in the first resurrection," over whom "the second death has no power" (20:6), and for a "share in the tree of life" (22:19). Verse 7 promises the faithful an inheritance; verse 8 names the other share.

a: the lake that burns with fire and sulfur
p: No. It describes people who refuse the cure that is offered free in the verses on either side.
b: Paul gives a similar list and then tells the Corinthians that some of them used to be these very things, "but you were washed" (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). Revelation's version of washing is "they washed their robes... in the blood of the Lamb" (7:14; 22:14). The free water of life is offered in 21:6, just before this verse, and again in 22:17. Even "Jezebel" was given time to repent (2:21). The people outside the city are not those who once sinned, but those who keep refusing to be washed (22:14–15). The chapter 21 page has a fuller discussion, including what "hell" does and doesn't mean in Revelation.

p: The synagogue paraphrases used it for final exclusion from the world to come.
b: The Aramaic Targums read in synagogues use "the second death" for final judgment after physical death. Targum Onkelos on Deuteronomy 33:6: "Let Reuben live, and not die the second death." The Targum of Jeremiah 51:39, 57 says Babylon's rulers "will die the second death and not live in the world to come." The Targums were written down after the first century, but they keep older synagogue wording. Revelation defines it: "This is the second death, the lake of fire" (20:14).

a: coming down out of heaven from God
t: Babel built up; Jerusalem comes down
p: People tried to build a city up to heaven. God sends one down.
b: At Babel people said, "Come on, let's build ourselves a city, and a tower with its head in the heavens. We will win a name for ourselves" (Genesis 11:4). The new Jerusalem is not built from below. It comes down "from God," and its citizens carry God's name, not their own (22:4). The fourfold list of "every tribe, language, people and nation" also undoes Babel's scattering. Others have noted the Babel contrast; I think it is the key to why the descent is mentioned twice (21:2, 10).

p: Ezekiel saw his temple city from a very high mountain. John saw Babylon from a wilderness.
b: In Ezekiel 40:2 the prophet says that in visions from God he was brought to the land of Israel and set down on a very tall mountain, and on it, toward the south, was what looked like a built city. Isaiah 2:2: the mountain of the LORD's house raised above the hills. John was carried "into a wilderness" to see Babylon (17:3); he is carried to a mountain to see the bride.

p: The one on the throne looked like jasper stone (4:3).
b: Jasper is the first stone named for God's appearance (4:3), the wall's material (21:18), and the first foundation (21:19). The city "had God's glory": it reflects the one who lives in it. Ancient jasper may have meant a clear, bright stone rather than the opaque jasper of today.

a: On the east were three gates
p: Israel camped around the tabernacle three tribes to a side.
b: Numbers 2 arranges the twelve tribes around the tabernacle, three on each side. Ezekiel's city has twelve gates named for the tribes, three on each side, and is named "The LORD is there" (Ezekiel 48:30–35). A Dead Sea Scrolls text, the "Description of the New Jerusalem," also imagines a measured city with twelve tribal gates.

p: In the prophets, measuring a place means God protects it.
b: Ezekiel's guide measures the temple with a rod (Ezekiel 40:3). Zechariah sees a man measure Jerusalem, and God promises to be "a wall of fire around it" (Zechariah 2:1–5). John measured the temple in 11:1 and left the outer court to be trampled. Now everything is measured, and nothing is left outside the protection.

a: The city lies in a square
p: Herodotus described ancient Babylon as a perfect square with a river through it.
b: Herodotus (Histories 1.178–180) said Babylon was a square, 120 stadia on each side, with a vast wall, a hundred bronze gates, and the Euphrates flowing through the middle. Ezekiel's city is a square too (Ezekiel 48:16). John's city is square in plan and as tall as it is wide, a cube like the Most Holy Place (1 Kings 6:20). See Claude's theory on the chapter page.

a: by human measure, which is the angel's measure
t: A hint to read the numbers?
p: 144 cubits is a tiny wall for a city 1,400 miles high. Both numbers are built on twelve.
b: 144 = 12 × 12, and 12,000 = 12 × 1,000. As a building, a 216-foot wall around a 1,400-mile-high city makes little sense, so many readers see the numbers as meaning more than blueprints. Literal readers take both as real measures (the wall may be its thickness). "Human measure, which is the angel's measure" may mean the angel's figures are given in our units so we can grasp them.

t: A city made of the Holy of Holies’ lining
p: Solomon overlaid the Most Holy Place with pure gold.
b: "Solomon covered the inside of the house with refined gold" (1 Kings 6:20–22). The whole city is made of what used to line God's private room. In the Roman world glass was a luxury, and perfectly clear glass was rare. Gold you can see through is not a real metal; it is a picture of perfect purity with nothing hidden.

a: The twelve gates were twelve pearls
p: Pliny said pearls held "the highest rank among all valuables." A rabbinic legend has huge single gems as Jerusalem’s gates.
b: Pliny the Elder (Natural History 9.106) ranked pearls above every other valuable. A later tradition in the Babylonian Talmud (Bava Batra 75a) says God will set gems 30 cubits across in Jerusalem's gates. Isaiah promises "your gates of sparkling stones" (Isaiah 54:12). Babylon's merchants lost their pearls (18:12, 16); here pearls are the way in.

a: The main street of the city was pure gold
p: Cities in Asia were built around one grand colonnaded street.
b: Greek and Roman cities had a main street (plateia, the word used here), often paved in marble and lined with columns. In Ephesus a marble street ran from the theater to the harbor (rebuilt around AD 400 as the Arcadian Way). This city's one street is gold, and the river of life flows down its middle (22:1–2).

a: Its gates will never be shut by day
p: Ancient cities shut their gates every night. This one has no night and no enemies.
b: City gates were locked at night against raiders and opened by day for trade (Nehemiah 7:3; 13:19). Isaiah 60:11: "Your gates will stand open all the time; day and night they will not be shut." With no night and no enemy, the wall marks belonging, not defense.

a: except those who are written in the Lamb's book of life
p: The entry list belongs to the Lamb, which is the answer to 21:8.
b: "Nothing common will ever enter" echoes Isaiah 52:1, a promise to Zion that the unclean "will never come into you again." Entry is decided by one register, "the Lamb's book of life," the book of the one who was slaughtered to buy people "from every tribe and language and people and nation" (5:9). Israel's promise is kept, and its gates are opened to the nations.

p: From Nebuchadnezzar’s boast in Daniel 4:30. Revelation gives her nine names in all.
b: In Daniel 4:30 the king looks over his capital and boasts that he built this great Babylon by his own strength, for the honor of his splendor. While the words were still in his mouth, he lost his kingdom and his mind. Revelation names Babylon six times and also calls her "the great city," "the mighty city," "the great prostitute," "the mother of prostitutes," "a mystery," "the woman" and "a queen." The chapter 18 page lists each with its source.

p: The real Babylon was mostly empty in the first century. The name meant a power, not a place.
b: Babylon on the Euphrates declined after the Seleucid kings built a new capital nearby around 300 BC. By the first century AD it was mostly deserted; Strabo quotes a poet: "The great city is a great desert" (Geography 16.1.5). So John's readers heard "Babylon" the way we might hear "Pharaoh": a famous past standing for something present. See the map on the chapter 18 page.

a: fine linen, purple, silk, and scarlet
p: Silk came from China, purple dye was among the costliest goods in the empire.
b: Silk reached Rome over the long trade routes from China, and the Roman writer Pliny complained that India, China and Arabia drained a hundred million sesterces a year from the empire for luxuries (Natural History 12.84). Tyrian purple was so costly that certain purple garments were reserved by law for the emperor and senators. "Fragrant wood" is citron wood, used for tables that cost as much as an estate.

a: dressed in fine linen, purple, and scarlet
t: Is Babylon Jerusalem? The Ezekiel 16 argument
p: Ezekiel dressed unfaithful Jerusalem in linen and gold, then had her lovers strip and burn her.
b: Ezekiel 16 pictures Jerusalem dressed by God in fine linen, embroidered cloth, gold and jewels (16:10–13). She turns to other lovers, who then strip off her clothes and burn her houses with fire (Ezekiel 16:37–41). Revelation 17:16 has the beast do the same to the prostitute. Many preterists read this as evidence that Babylon is first-century Jerusalem. Others note that most of chapter 18's wording comes from the songs over Babylon and Tyre instead. The Bible never calls Jerusalem "Babylon" outright.

a: In her was found the blood of prophets
p: Jesus said the blood of the prophets would fall on Jerusalem. By early tradition, Rome killed Peter and Paul.
b: Jesus to Jerusalem: "all the righteous blood poured out on the earth will come on you" (Matthew 23:35–37). Preterists hear this verse as Jerusalem's judgment. But Rome killed Christians under Nero (Tacitus, Annals 15.44), and the verse widens to "all who have been slaughtered on the earth," which sounds like every violent empire. Idealists see the whole history of oppression gathered into one city.

p: Women prophesied in the early church. The issue is her message, not that she is a woman.
b: Women prophets were known and honored in the early church: Philip's four daughters (Acts 21:9), and Paul's instructions for women who pray and prophesy (1 Corinthians 11:5). Jesus does not fault her for prophesying. He faults what she teaches, and the church for leaving her alone. "Calls herself" is the same complaint as 2:2, those "who call themselves apostles and are not."

p: From the word for prostitute. In the prophets it is the standard picture for idolatry.
b: The verb comes from pornē, "prostitute." By John's day it covered any sexual sin, but in the Greek Old Testament the same word family translates Hebrew zanah, which the prophets use for Israel worshiping other gods (Jeremiah 3:1; Ezekiel 16; Hosea 1–3). Here it is paired with idol food, exactly as in the Baal of Peor story (Numbers 25:1–2) and the Jerusalem council's letter (Acts 15:29). Whether it is literal, figurative or both is debated; see the chapter 2 page.

p: Thyatira’s trade guilds met for meals honoring their patron gods.
b: Thyatira's inscriptions name a remarkable number of guilds: wool, linen, dyers, leather, tanners, potters, bakers, bronze smiths, slave dealers. Guild members met for banquets, often in temple dining rooms, eating meat from the sacrifices. A Christian who stayed away could lose business. Paul's long answer to the same problem is 1 Corinthians 8–10.

p: Even "Jezebel" gets a chance. The original queen did not.
b: Jesus has already given her time, and the warning that follows is still conditional: "unless they repent of her works" (2:22). Peter says the Lord is patient because he does not want anyone to be lost (2 Peter 3:9). Compare the plagues, where people "did not repent" (9:20–21; 16:9, 11).

p: The Greek says only "bed." It was also the word for a banquet couch.
b: Klinē means a bed or the couch diners reclined on. The KJV and this site have "bed"; many modern versions say "sickbed" or "bed of suffering," taking the sense from the sickness and death that follow. Some commentators hear a deliberate turn: the banquet couch of the idol feast becomes a bed of sickness. Ancient invitations spoke of dining "at the couch of the lord Sarapis."

p: Adultery assumes a marriage. Her followers already belong to Christ.
b: Jezebel is charged with porneia, but her followers with moicheia, adultery: the betrayal of a spouse. In the prophets, God is Israel's husband (Hosea 2:19–20; Jeremiah 3:20), and in the New Testament Christ is the church's (2 Corinthians 11:2; Revelation 19:7). James uses the same picture when he calls his readers adulteresses, because friendship with the world is hostility toward God (James 4:4).

p: Her followers, the people she taught. Not literally her sons and daughters.
b: In the Bible a teacher's disciples are often called children (1 John 2:1; 3 John 4; Galatians 4:19). "I will put her children to death" is literally "I will kill her children with death"; in the Greek Old Testament "death" often means plague (compare 6:8). Some take it as a coming epidemic, others as spiritual death.

a: I am not putting any other burden on you
p: Echoes Acts 15:28, which also banned idol food and sexual immorality.
b: The council's letter to gentile believers: "For the Holy Spirit has decided, and so have we, to place no heavier load on you than these necessary things: keep away from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled and from sexual sin" (Acts 15:28–29). The Greek word for that "load" is baros, the same word Jesus uses here for "burden." Jesus's word to the faithful in Thyatira sounds like the same agreement: keep those basics, and nothing more is required.

a: those who call themselves apostles and are not
p: Wandering teachers claimed to be apostles. Churches tested them, and Ephesus was good at it.
b: "Apostle" means "one who is sent." Besides the Twelve and Paul, the early church used it for traveling missionaries, and some were frauds (2 Corinthians 11:13). The Didache, a church manual from about this time, says a true apostle stays a day or two; "if he stays three days, he is a false prophet," and if he asks for money, he is a false prophet (11.5–6). Ignatius later praised Ephesus for not letting false teachers "sow among you" (To the Ephesians 9.1). This is the first of the "say they are... and are not" claims in the letters.

a: those who say they are Jews and are not
t: "Say they are Jews and are not"
p: A painful phrase about a local quarrel over a name that was also a legal status. Not a verdict on the Jewish people.
b: Being a "Jew" in the empire carried legal standing: Jews were generally allowed to refuse the city and imperial sacrifices (a tolerated custom more than a formal exemption), and after AD 70 they paid a special tax. Who counted was argued in courts as well as synagogues, the way false claims to Roman citizenship could be punished by death (Suetonius, Claudius 25.3). Many think members of Smyrna's synagogue were denouncing the believers, perhaps to the authorities; the Martyrdom of Polycarp (12–13) later tells of Smyrna's Jews joining the crowd against Polycarp, though that account has its own slant. John, a Jew, denies these accusers the name because they side against Israel's Messiah, as Paul says real Jewishness is inward (Romans 2:28–29). Some scholars think they were gentiles claiming Jewish status. The phrase was later used to justify hatred of Jews, which the text does not support. See the topic page for the views.
orig: τῶν λεγόντων Ἰουδαίους εἶναι ἑαυτούς, καὶ οὐκ εἰσίν

p: Jesus calls himself true just before exposing those who "are lying" (3:9).
b: Ho alēthinos, "the true one, the genuine one," is set against the claimants in 3:9 who "say they are Jews and are not, but are lying." Real versus counterfeit is one of Revelation's main threads: compare "the witness who is faithful and true" (3:14) and the rider called "Faithful and True" (19:11).

p: Only Philadelphia’s version adds "lying," the word Revelation uses for false loyalty.
b: In Revelation, lying is mostly about allegiance: false apostles are "liars" (2:2), of the 144,000 "Not one lie was found in their mouths" (14:5), and "all liars" are outside the city (21:8; 22:15). The pairing of Satan and lying echoes Jesus in John 8:44: the devil "is a liar and the father of falsehood." See the topic page for the whole pattern.

p: The last of the "you say... but" claims, this time made by a whole church.
b: Laodicea was proud of its wealth. After an earthquake in AD 60 it rebuilt without help from Rome (Tacitus, Annals 14.27). The church took on the city's self-image. Jesus answers the claim the way he answered the false apostles and false Jews: with what is really true, "poor, blind, and naked," and then with an offer of real gold, clothes and eye salve (3:18). Compare Babylon: "I sit as a queen" (18:7).
